about: A shared UK-wide revision pack on the heart and lungs, used by several medical schools and years rather than written for one university's syllabus. It runs from structure and function (cardiac cycle, conduction, blood pressure, mechanics of breathing, gas exchange) through the causes and risk factors of common diseases, core clinical skills and function tests (ECG, spirometry, arterial blood gases, examination), the mechanisms of the main drug classes, and an introduction to clinical decision-making. Topics are mapped to the cardiovascular and respiratory areas of the GMC's MLA content map, and guideline points follow current UK guidance (NICE, BTS/NICE/SIGN, RCP, Resuscitation Council UK) as checked in October 2026. Earlier-year students can focus on the physiology and mechanisms; clinical-year students should work through the interpretation items and cases. This pack is educational revision material, not clinical advice, and gives no drug doses.

notes.h: Cardiorespiratory structure and function: pump, vessels, lungs and gas transport
notes.overview: The heart is two pumps in series driven by its own pacemaker; blood pressure is set by cardiac output and resistance; the lungs move air by changing volume and exchange gas by diffusion. This topic gives the physiology that every later cardiorespiratory topic, test and drug relies on.
objectives: Explain the ionic basis of the SA node pacemaker potential and the ventricular action potential.
Apply CO = HR × SV, MAP ≈ CO × TPR and Poiseuille’s relationship to predict haemodynamic changes.
Explain the baroreceptor reflex and Starling forces, and use them to explain postural symptoms and oedema.
Distinguish the Bohr and Haldane effects and interpret shifts of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve.
Calculate alveolar ventilation and cardiac output (Fick) from given values.

sections.h: Heart structure, cardiac cycle and conduction
sections.body:
The right heart pumps blood to the lungs and the left heart to the body. Atrioventricular valves (tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left) stop backflow into the atria; semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) stop backflow into the ventricles.
- S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole; S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the start of diastole. S2 normally splits on inspiration because more blood returns to the right heart and pulmonary closure is delayed.
- Conduction: SA node → atria → AV node → bundle of His → left and right bundle branches → Purkinje fibres. The AV node delays conduction (roughly 0.1 s, approximate) so the atria can finish filling the ventricles, and it limits how many fast atrial impulses reach the ventricles.
- SA node: a slow pacemaker depolarisation (the 'funny' current, If, through HCN channels, then T-type Ca²⁺ entry) reaches threshold, and the upstroke is carried by L-type Ca²⁺ channels, not fast Na⁺ channels. Sympathetic β1 stimulation steepens the slope; vagal acetylcholine flattens it.
- Ventricular myocytes: fast Na⁺ entry (phase 0), a Ca²⁺ plateau (phase 2) and a long refractory period, so cardiac muscle cannot be tetanised.
- Excitation–contraction coupling: Ca²⁺ entry triggers Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (RyR2); relaxation needs SERCA reuptake and the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger.

sections.h: Cardiac output, blood pressure and fluid exchange
sections.body:
- Cardiac output (CO) = heart rate × stroke volume, about 5 L/min at rest (approximate). Stroke volume rises with preload (Frank–Starling: more stretch, stronger contraction) and contractility, and falls with afterload.
- Mean arterial pressure ≈ CO × total peripheral resistance (TPR); at rest it can be estimated as diastolic pressure + ⅓ of the pulse pressure.
- Poiseuille: resistance = 8ηL ÷ πr⁴. Because of the fourth power, small changes in arteriolar radius control resistance and the distribution of flow; halving the radius raises resistance 16-fold.
- Baroreceptor reflex: stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (glossopharyngeal nerve, IX) and aortic arch (vagus, X) signal to the nucleus tractus solitarius. A fall in pressure reduces their firing, so sympathetic outflow rises and vagal outflow falls: faster heart, stronger contraction, arteriolar and venous constriction.
- Left ventricular coronary flow occurs mainly in diastole, so tachycardia shortens supply time while raising demand.
- Starling forces: capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, plasma oncotic pressure (mostly albumin) holds it in, and lymphatics return the small excess. Oedema follows a raised venous or capillary pressure (e.g. heart failure), low albumin, lymphatic blockage or leaky capillaries.

sections.h: Ventilation, gas exchange and gas transport
sections.body:
- Quiet inspiration is active: the diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3–C5) and external intercostals enlarge the thorax, alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric (Boyle's law) and air flows in. Quiet expiration is passive elastic recoil.
- Type I pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface; type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant. Surfactant lowers surface tension most in small alveoli, so by Laplace (P = 2T/r) small alveoli do not empty into large ones, and compliance rises.
- Compliance (ΔV/ΔP) falls in fibrosis (stiff lungs) and rises in emphysema (floppy lungs with poor recoil).
- Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × respiratory rate. Diffusion (Fick's law) is proportional to area × partial pressure gradient ÷ membrane thickness.
- Both ventilation and perfusion are greater at the lung base than the apex when upright, but perfusion changes more, so V/Q is high at the apex and low at the base. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli.
- The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid because binding is cooperative. Raised PCO₂ and H⁺ (the Bohr effect), temperature and 2,3-BPG shift it right, helping oxygen unloading in active tissue.
- Most CO₂ travels as bicarbonate made by carbonic anhydrase in red cells; deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO₂ (the Haldane effect).
- Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to CSF H⁺ generated from arterial CO₂ and provide most of the resting drive; peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) respond strongly once PaO₂ falls below about 8 kPa (approximate).

- Fick principle: cardiac output = oxygen consumption ÷ (arterial − mixed venous O₂ content). With VO₂ 300 mL/min, CaO₂ 200 mL/L and CvO₂ 150 mL/L: 300 ÷ 50 = 6 L/min. If output falls while VO₂ is unchanged, tissues extract more oxygen and CvO₂ falls.
- Alveolar ventilation: tidal volume 500 mL at 12/min with 150 mL dead space gives (500 − 150) × 12 = 4.2 L/min. Rapid shallow breathing at 250 mL × 24/min keeps minute ventilation at 6 L/min but alveolar ventilation falls to (250 − 150) × 24 = 2.4 L/min.
- MAP: blood pressure 120/80 mmHg gives about 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg.

A 25-year-old loses about 1.5 L of blood after a femoral fracture. Venous return and preload fall, so stroke volume falls (Frank–Starling). Reduced baroreceptor firing raises sympathetic outflow: heart rate climbs, contractility rises, arterioles constrict (raising TPR) and veins constrict to return blood to the heart. Systolic pressure may be nearly normal at first while the pulse pressure narrows, which is why a rising heart rate is an early warning sign. Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls, so fluid moves from the interstitium into the plasma. If loss continues, compensation fails, pressure falls and organ perfusion suffers.

- Students often think the SA node upstroke is a Na⁺ spike. It is carried by L-type Ca²⁺ channels, which is why rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers slow nodal tissue.
- Students often think the lung apex is better perfused. Perfusion is greatest at the base; the apex has the highest V/Q ratio.
- Students often think pulmonary vessels dilate in hypoxia, as systemic ones do. They constrict, matching perfusion to ventilation (and, when widespread, raising pulmonary artery pressure).
- Students often think a normal blood pressure rules out significant blood loss. Baroreflex compensation can hold pressure up until a late stage; tachycardia and a narrow pulse pressure appear earlier.

notes.h: Causes and risk factors of common cardiorespiratory disease
notes.overview: Most heart and lung disease in the UK grows from a small set of mechanisms: atherosclerosis, raised blood pressure, thrombosis, and chronic airway inflammation or destruction. This topic links each mechanism to its modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors and to how UK practice estimates and reduces risk.
objectives: Explain how an atherosclerotic plaque forms and why some plaques rupture.
Distinguish modifiable from non-modifiable risk factors and calculate pack-years.
Apply Virchow's triad to venous thromboembolism and to stroke in atrial fibrillation.
Explain how smoking and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency cause emphysema, and how asthma differs.
Interpret a 10-year cardiovascular risk estimate in the light of current NICE guidance.

sections.body:
Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial dysfunction (from smoking, hypertension, high LDL, diabetes). LDL enters the intima and is oxidised; monocytes migrate in and become macrophages that take up oxidised LDL to form foam cells (the fatty streak). Smooth muscle cells migrate and lay down collagen as a fibrous cap over a lipid-rich, partly necrotic core.
- Stable plaques with thick caps narrow the lumen and limit flow only when demand rises, causing stable angina.
- Vulnerable plaques have thin caps, large lipid cores and many inflammatory cells. Rupture or erosion exposes thrombogenic material, and the resulting thrombus causes an acute coronary syndrome or ischaemic stroke.
- A plaque does not need to cause a tight stenosis to rupture; many infarcts arise from lesions that were not flow-limiting.

sections.h: Thrombosis, blood pressure and airway disease
sections.body:
- Virchow's triad: stasis, hypercoagulability and vessel wall (endothelial) injury. Venous thromboembolism risks include surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy and the postpartum period, oestrogen-containing medicines, previous VTE and inherited thrombophilias such as factor V Leiden.
- In atrial fibrillation, the atria do not contract effectively, blood stagnates (especially in the left atrial appendage), and thrombus can embolise to the brain.
- Most hypertension is essential (primary). Secondary causes include kidney disease, renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's syndrome and coarctation of the aorta.
- COPD: in the UK, mainly smoking. Proteases released by inflammatory cells outweigh antiproteases, destroying alveolar walls (emphysema) and removing the elastic recoil and radial traction that hold small airways open. Smoking-related emphysema is usually centriacinar and upper-zone; emphysema in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is typically panacinar and basal. Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as a productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years.
- Asthma: chronic airway inflammation, often allergic, involving IgE-sensitised mast cells, eosinophils and Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13), with variable, reversible airflow obstruction. Triggers include viral infections, allergens, exercise, cold air and, in some people, NSAIDs or β-blockers.

- Non-modifiable: age, male sex, family history of premature cardiovascular disease, ethnicity, inherited conditions such as familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
- Modifiable: smoking, hypertension, raised LDL or non-HDL cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, excess alcohol, and occupational or environmental exposures.
- Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked. 20 a day from 17 to 62 = 1 × 45 = 45 pack-years.
- FH is usually autosomal dominant (variants in LDLR, most often, or APOB or PCSK9). It causes very high LDL from birth, tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease. Each first-degree relative has a 50% chance of carrying it, so relatives should be tested (cascade testing).
- Lung cancer: smoking is the main cause; passive smoking, radon, asbestos and air pollution also contribute.

- Risk is estimated, not measured. In UK primary care a 10-year risk score combines age, sex, ethnicity, deprivation, smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol ratio, BMI, diabetes, family history and several conditions and medicines.
- Lipid profile: total cholesterol, HDL, non-HDL (total minus HDL) and, from these, LDL. A total cholesterol above about 7.5 mmol/L with a family history of early coronary disease should raise suspicion of FH (approximate).
- Spirometry identifies airflow obstruction in COPD; serum alpha-1 antitrypsin is checked when emphysema starts early, in someone with little smoking history, or with a family history.
- Ultrasound screening finds abdominal aortic aneurysms before they rupture: in England, men are invited in the year they turn 65.

- NICE NG238 (published December 2023, minor changes 2025) uses QRISK3 for adults aged 25 to 84 without cardiovascular disease. A risk tool is not used for people already at high risk: type 1 diabetes, eGFR below 60 and/or albuminuria, or FH and other inherited lipid disorders.
- A statin is offered for primary prevention when the 10-year QRISK3 risk is 10% or more, after lifestyle advice; NICE says a statin should not be ruled out below 10% if the person prefers one or their risk may be underestimated.
- NICE NG115 (COPD) emphasises recording pack-years and offering help to stop smoking at every opportunity; stopping is the most effective way to slow the decline in lung function.
- NHS AAA screening invites men in England in the year they turn 65.
Check the current NICE guidance and screening pages, which are updated over time.

A 34-year-old man's father died of a myocardial infarction at 46. His total cholesterol is 9.2 mmol/L and his Achilles tendons are thickened. Familial hypercholesterolaemia is likely: a dominant variant (most often in the LDL receptor gene) means the liver clears LDL poorly, so LDL is high from birth and atherosclerosis starts early. Because his risk is high whatever a population score predicts, a risk tool such as QRISK3 is not used to decide on treatment, and specialist assessment with genetic testing is appropriate. His children and siblings each have a 50% chance of carrying the variant, so cascade testing of relatives matters as much as his own treatment.

- Students often think the tightest stenosis is the one most likely to cause a heart attack. Rupture depends on plaque composition (thin cap, large lipid core, inflammation), not just on narrowing.
- Students often link panacinar, basal emphysema to smoking. That pattern points to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; smoking typically causes centriacinar, upper-zone disease.

notes.body:
Atherosclerosis and plaque rupture
Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial dysfunction (from smoking, hypertension, high LDL, diabetes). LDL enters the intima and is oxidised; monocytes migrate in and become macrophages that take up oxidised LDL to form foam cells (the fatty streak). Smooth muscle cells migrate and lay down collagen as a fibrous cap over a lipid-rich, partly necrotic core.
- Stable plaques with thick caps narrow the lumen and limit flow only when demand rises, causing stable angina.
- Vulnerable plaques have thin caps, large lipid cores and many inflammatory cells. Rupture or erosion exposes thrombogenic material, and the resulting thrombus causes an acute coronary syndrome or ischaemic stroke.
- A plaque does not need to cause a tight stenosis to rupture; many infarcts arise from lesions that were not flow-limiting.

Thrombosis, blood pressure and airway disease
- Virchow's triad: stasis, hypercoagulability and vessel wall (endothelial) injury. Venous thromboembolism risks include surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy and the postpartum period, oestrogen-containing medicines, previous VTE and inherited thrombophilias such as factor V Leiden.
- In atrial fibrillation, the atria do not contract effectively, blood stagnates (especially in the left atrial appendage), and thrombus can embolise to the brain.
- Most hypertension is essential (primary). Secondary causes include kidney disease, renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's syndrome and coarctation of the aorta.
- COPD: in the UK, mainly smoking. Proteases released by inflammatory cells outweigh antiproteases, destroying alveolar walls (emphysema) and removing the elastic recoil and radial traction that hold small airways open. Smoking-related emphysema is usually centriacinar and upper-zone; emphysema in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is typically panacinar and basal. Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as a productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years.
- Asthma: chronic airway inflammation, often allergic, involving IgE-sensitised mast cells, eosinophils and Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13), with variable, reversible airflow obstruction. Triggers include viral infections, allergens, exercise, cold air and, in some people, NSAIDs or β-blockers.

- Non-modifiable: age, male sex, family history of premature cardiovascular disease, ethnicity, inherited conditions such as familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
- Modifiable: smoking, hypertension, raised LDL or non-HDL cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, excess alcohol, and occupational or environmental exposures.
- Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked. 20 a day from 17 to 62 = 1 × 45 = 45 pack-years.
- FH is usually autosomal dominant (variants in LDLR, most often, or APOB or PCSK9). It causes very high LDL from birth, tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease. Each first-degree relative has a 50% chance of carrying it, so relatives should be tested (cascade testing).
- Lung cancer: smoking is the main cause; passive smoking, radon, asbestos and air pollution also contribute.

- Risk is estimated, not measured. In UK primary care a 10-year risk score combines age, sex, ethnicity, deprivation, smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol ratio, BMI, diabetes, family history and several conditions and medicines.
- Lipid profile: total cholesterol, HDL, non-HDL (total minus HDL) and, from these, LDL. A total cholesterol above about 7.5 mmol/L with a family history of early coronary disease should raise suspicion of FH (approximate).
- Spirometry identifies airflow obstruction in COPD; serum alpha-1 antitrypsin is checked when emphysema starts early, in someone with little smoking history, or with a family history.
- Ultrasound screening finds abdominal aortic aneurysms before they rupture: in England, men are invited in the year they turn 65.

- A statin is offered for primary prevention when the 10-year QRISK3 risk is 10% or more, after lifestyle advice; NICE says a statin should not be ruled out below 10% if the person prefers one or their risk may be underestimated.
- NICE NG115 (COPD) emphasises recording pack-years and offering help to stop smoking at every opportunity; stopping is the most effective way to slow the decline in lung function.
- NHS AAA screening invites men in England in the year they turn 65.
Check the current NICE guidance and screening pages, which are updated over time.

A 34-year-old man's father died of a myocardial infarction at 46. His total cholesterol is 9.2 mmol/L and his Achilles tendons are thickened. Familial hypercholesterolaemia is likely: a dominant variant (most often in the LDL receptor gene) means the liver clears LDL poorly, so LDL is high from birth and atherosclerosis starts early. Because his risk is high whatever a population score predicts, a risk tool such as QRISK3 is not used to decide on treatment, and specialist assessment with genetic testing is appropriate. notes.h: Clinical skills and function tests: examination, ECG, spirometry and blood gases
notes.overview: Examination findings and simple tests are applied physiology. This topic covers the cardiovascular and respiratory examination, reading a rhythm strip and 12-lead ECG, spirometry patterns, arterial blood gases and the blood tests most used in chest pain and breathlessness.
objectives: Interpret chest examination findings in consolidation, effusion, pneumothorax and collapse.

Distinguish obstructive and restrictive spirometry using the FEV₁/FVC ratio.

sections.body:
- Heart sounds: S1 (mitral and tricuspid closure), S2 (aortic and pulmonary closure, splitting on inspiration). Murmurs: aortic stenosis is ejection systolic and radiates to the carotids; mitral regurgitation is pansystolic and radiates to the axilla; aortic regurgitation is early diastolic at the left sternal edge (best heard sitting forward in held expiration); mitral stenosis is a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex (best in the left lateral position).
- Jugular venous pressure reflects right atrial pressure; it is measured as the vertical height above the sternal angle with the patient at 45° and is typically up to about 3–4 cm (approximate).
- Chest percussion: dull in consolidation and collapse, stony dull in pleural effusion, hyper-resonant in pneumothorax. Consolidation transmits sound well (bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance); fluid and air reduce it.
- The trachea is pushed away from a tension pneumothorax or a massive effusion, and pulled towards lobar collapse or upper-lobe fibrosis.
- Clubbing is not caused by COPD itself; new clubbing in COPD should prompt a search for another cause such as lung cancer.

- Standard paper runs at 25 mm/s: one small square = 0.04 s; one large square (5 small) = 0.2 s.
- Rate in a regular rhythm = 300 ÷ large squares between R waves (or 1,500 ÷ small squares). For an irregular rhythm, count QRS complexes on a 10-second strip and multiply by 6.

- Atrial fibrillation: no organised P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm.
- Territories: inferior leads (II, III, aVF) are usually supplied by the right coronary artery (sometimes the circumflex), with reciprocal change in aVL; anterior V1–V4 by the left anterior descending; lateral I, aVL, V5–V6 by the circumflex or diagonal branches. sections.h: What spirometry, blood gases and blood tests measure
sections.body:
- Obstruction: FEV₁/FVC below 0.7 (or below the lower limit of normal). Restriction: FVC reduced with a normal or raised ratio (e.g. fibrosis, chest wall disease). Gas transfer (TLCO) falls with loss of alveolar–capillary surface (emphysema, fibrosis, pulmonary vascular disease) and in anaemia.
- ABG (typical adult ranges, vary by lab): pH 7.35–7.45; PaO₂ about 11–13 kPa on air; PaCO₂ 4.7–6.0 kPa; HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mmol/L. Interpret in order: oxygenation (and FiO₂), pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻, then compensation.
- Respiratory failure: PaO₂ below 8 kPa. Type 1 has a normal or low PaCO₂ (V/Q mismatch, e.g. pneumonia, PE); type 2 has PaCO₂ above about 6.0 kPa (alveolar hypoventilation, e.g. COPD, opioids, neuromuscular weakness).
- On air at sea level, alveolar PO₂ ≈ 20 − PaCO₂/0.8 kPa (approximate). A raised A–a gradient means a gas-exchange problem; hypoventilation alone gives a normal gradient.
- Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); a raised gap in metabolic acidosis suggests added acid (ketones, lactate, toxins, renal failure).
- Troponin rises and falls in myocardial infarction but is also raised by PE, sepsis, myocarditis, heart failure and kidney disease. A normal natriuretic peptide (BNP or NT-proBNP) makes heart failure unlikely. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific for VTE.
- Pulse oximetry does not measure CO₂, reads falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning, and can overestimate saturation in people with darker skin.

notes.h: Drug treatment of heart and lung disease: classes and mechanisms
notes.overview: Most cardiorespiratory drugs act on a small number of targets: the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, adrenoceptors, ion channels, platelets and clotting factors, cholesterol synthesis, and airway smooth muscle and inflammation. Knowing the target predicts both the benefit and the main adverse effects. No doses are given; use the BNF.
objectives: Explain the mechanism and main adverse effects of each major cardiovascular and respiratory drug class.
Distinguish antiplatelet from anticoagulant drugs and explain why aspirin’s effect outlasts the drug.
Explain why some drugs in heart failure improve survival while others mainly relieve symptoms.
Apply current UK guidance on the first step for hypertension, HFrEF and newly diagnosed asthma.
Recognise dangerous combinations, such as a β-blocker with verapamil, and digoxin with hypokalaemia.

sections.body:
- ACE inhibitors (e.g. ramipril) block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, causing vasodilation and less aldosterone. ACE also breaks down bradykinin, which accumulates and causes dry cough and, rarely, angioedema. Other effects: hyperkalaemia and a fall in kidney function. Avoided in pregnancy.
- Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs, e.g. losartan) block AT1 receptors: similar benefits with little cough. An ACE inhibitor and an ARB are not combined.
- β-blockers reduce heart rate, contractility and renin release, lowering myocardial oxygen demand. Non-selective agents also block airway β2 receptors and can cause bronchospasm in asthma.
- Calcium-channel blockers: dihydropyridines (amlodipine) mainly dilate arterioles; ankle oedema is common and does not respond to diuretics. Rate-limiting agents (verapamil, diltiazem) also slow the SA and AV nodes.
- Diuretics: thiazide-like (indapamide) block the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule; loop diuretics (furosemide) block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Both can cause hypokalaemia.
- Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase; liver cells make more LDL receptors and clear more LDL. Muscle aches are the best-known adverse effect.
- Nitrates (e.g. GTN) release nitric oxide, raising cGMP and dilating mainly veins, which lowers preload and myocardial oxygen demand. Headache and hypotension are common; they must not be combined with PDE5 inhibitors (e.g. sildenafil).

- Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, blocking thromboxane A₂ for the platelet’s lifetime (platelets have no nucleus to make new enzyme). P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor) block ADP-induced activation; aspirin with a P2Y12 inhibitor is dual antiplatelet therapy after ACS.
- Anticoagulants act on clotting factors: warfarin antagonises vitamin K-dependent synthesis (monitored by INR); direct oral anticoagulants inhibit factor Xa (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or thrombin (dabigatran).
- Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) block aldosterone; SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g. dapagliflozin) increase urinary glucose and sodium loss and improve heart failure outcomes. Sacubitril/valsartan (an ARNI) adds neprilysin inhibition to an ARB and must not be given with an ACE inhibitor.
- Digoxin inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (raising intracellular Ca²⁺) and increases vagal tone, slowing AV conduction. Hypokalaemia, kidney impairment and some interacting drugs (e.g. amiodarone) increase toxicity.
- Vaughan Williams classes of antiarrhythmics: I Na⁺ channel block; II β-blockers; III K⁺ channel block (amiodarone, which can affect thyroid, lungs and liver); IV rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers. Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node to terminate re-entrant SVT.
- Airways: β2 agonists raise cAMP and relax bronchial smooth muscle (tremor, tachycardia, hypokalaemia); formoterol is long-acting but fast in onset. Muscarinic antagonists (ipratropium, tiotropium) block M3 receptors. Inhaled corticosteroids suppress airway inflammation by changing gene transcription. Leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast) block CysLT1.

- Verapamil with a β-blocker: additive AV block, bradycardia, hypotension and heart failure; intravenous verapamil with an intravenous β-blocker is contraindicated.
- ACE inhibitors, ARBs, MRAs and potassium-sparing diuretics raise potassium; check potassium and kidney function when starting or changing them.
- Loop or thiazide diuretics lower potassium, which increases digoxin toxicity (nausea, confusion, visual disturbance, arrhythmias).
- Non-selective β-blockers can provoke bronchospasm in asthma.
- Nitrates with PDE5 inhibitors can cause profound hypotension.
- Anticoagulants and antiplatelets increase bleeding; combining them multiplies the risk, so combinations are given for limited, defined periods.

- Hypertension (NICE NG136, last updated February 2026): step 1 is an ACE inhibitor or ARB for adults with type 2 diabetes, and for adults under 55 not of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin. A calcium-channel blocker is offered first to adults aged 55 or over, and to adults of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin, without type 2 diabetes. For people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin, consider an ARB in preference to an ACE inhibitor.
- HFrEF (NICE NG106, updated September 2025; HFrEF means LVEF 40% or less): offer an ACE inhibitor, a β-blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor, deciding timing and optimisation for the individual rather than in a fixed sequence; consider replacing the ACE inhibitor with an ARNI if symptoms persist. Diuretics relieve congestion at the lowest effective dose.
- Atrial fibrillation (NICE NG196): offer anticoagulation (a DOAC) when CHA₂DS₂-VASc is 2 or more, consider it for men scoring 1, and do not use aspirin alone for stroke prevention.
- Asthma (BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024): never a SABA without an inhaled corticosteroid. Newly diagnosed people aged 12 and over start as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol (AIR); those highly symptomatic or presenting with a severe exacerbation start low-dose MART, and uncontrolled asthma on AIR steps up to MART.
- COPD (NICE NG115): short-acting bronchodilator first; an inhaled corticosteroid only where there are asthmatic or steroid-responsive features.
- Oxygen (BTS 2017): target 94–98% for most, 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.

A 76-year-old man with heart failure takes digoxin. After a large increase in his loop diuretic he becomes nauseated and confused, with frequent ventricular ectopics. Diuretic-induced hypokalaemia means less K⁺ competes with digoxin for its binding site on Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, so digoxin binds more and its effect, and toxicity, increase. Recognising the mechanism points to the response: check potassium, kidney function and a digoxin level, and review the drugs. The same reasoning explains why potassium is monitored whenever diuretics, ACE inhibitors or MRAs are changed.

- Students often think aspirin is an anticoagulant. It is an antiplatelet drug; anticoagulants act on clotting factors.
- Students often think the drugs that relieve symptoms in heart failure are the ones that prolong life. Loop diuretics relieve congestion but have not been shown to improve survival; neurohormonal blockers and SGLT2 inhibitors do.
- Students often think β-blockers are always harmful in heart failure because they reduce contractility. Selected β-blockers, started cautiously, improve survival in HFrEF by blocking chronic sympathetic overstimulation.
- Students often think a SABA alone is reasonable long-term asthma treatment. Current UK guidance advises against SABA without an inhaled corticosteroid.
- Students often think ankle swelling on amlodipine means heart failure. It comes from arteriolar dilation raising capillary pressure, and diuretics do not relieve it.

- Anticoagulants and antiplatelets increase bleeding; combining them multiplies the risk, so combinations are given for limited, defined periods.

Guideline principles (England), no doses
- Hypertension (NICE NG136, last updated February 2026): step 1 is an ACE inhibitor or ARB for adults with type 2 diabetes, and for adults under 55 not of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin. A calcium-channel blocker is offered first to adults aged 55 or over, and to adults of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin, without type 2 diabetes. For people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin, consider an ARB in preference to an ACE inhibitor.
- HFrEF (NICE NG106, updated September 2025; HFrEF means LVEF 40% or less): offer an ACE inhibitor, a β-blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor, deciding timing and optimisation for the individual rather than in a fixed sequence; consider replacing the ACE inhibitor with an ARNI if symptoms persist. Diuretics relieve congestion at the lowest effective dose.
- Atrial fibrillation (NICE NG196): offer anticoagulation (a DOAC) when CHA₂DS₂-VASc is 2 or more, consider it for men scoring 1, and do not use aspirin alone for stroke prevention.
- Asthma (BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024): never a SABA without an inhaled corticosteroid. Newly diagnosed people aged 12 and over start as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol (AIR); those highly symptomatic or presenting with a severe exacerbation start low-dose MART, and uncontrolled asthma on AIR steps up to MART.
- COPD (NICE NG115): short-acting bronchodilator first; an inhaled corticosteroid only where there are asthmatic or steroid-responsive features.
- Oxygen (BTS 2017): target 94–98% for most, 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.

Clinical application
A 76-year-old man with heart failure takes digoxin. After a large increase in his loop diuretic he becomes nauseated and confused, with frequent ventricular ectopics. Diuretic-induced hypokalaemia means less K⁺ competes with digoxin for its binding site on Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, so digoxin binds more and its effect, and toxicity, increase. Recognising the mechanism points to the response: check potassium, kidney function and a digoxin level, and review the drugs. The same reasoning explains why potassium is monitored whenever diuretics, ACE inhibitors or MRAs are changed.

Common misconceptions
- Students often think aspirin is an anticoagulant. It is an antiplatelet drug; anticoagulants act on clotting factors.
- Students often think the drugs that relieve symptoms in heart failure are the ones that prolong life. Loop diuretics relieve congestion but have not been shown to improve survival; neurohormonal blockers and SGLT2 inhibitors do.
- Students often think β-blockers are always harmful in heart failure because they reduce contractility. Selected β-blockers, started cautiously, improve survival in HFrEF by blocking chronic sympathetic overstimulation.
- Students often think a SABA alone is reasonable long-term asthma treatment. Current UK guidance advises against SABA without an inhaled corticosteroid.
- Students often think ankle swelling on amlodipine means heart failure. It comes from arteriolar dilation raising capillary pressure, and diuretics do not relieve it.

notes.h: Clinical decision-making: probability, scores and bias
notes.overview: Good decisions combine a structured assessment, an understanding of how tests change probability, validated risk scores, awareness of thinking errors and shared decisions with patients. This topic uses cardiorespiratory examples: chest pain, suspected PE, pneumonia, atrial fibrillation and the deteriorating patient.
objectives: Calculate sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and likelihood ratios from a 2 × 2 table, and explain the effect of prevalence.
Calculate absolute and relative risk reduction and number needed to treat.
Apply NEWS2, CURB65, the two-level PE Wells score and CHA₂DS₂-VASc as UK guidance uses them.
Recognise anchoring, premature closure and availability bias and describe strategies against them.
Explain the principles of the ABCDE approach and shared decision-making.

sections.body:
- Most diagnoses come from the history. A differential lists possible causes ordered by likelihood and by how dangerous they would be to miss.
- Chest pain: dangerous causes to exclude early include acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade and oesophageal rupture.
- Breathlessness: cardiac (heart failure, arrhythmia), respiratory (asthma, COPD, pneumonia, PE, pneumothorax, fibrosis) and other (anaemia, metabolic acidosis, anxiety, which is a diagnosis of exclusion).
- Clinical reasoning uses fast pattern recognition (System 1), checked by slower analytical thinking (System 2) when the picture does not fit or the stakes are high.
- Thinking errors: anchoring (sticking to the first impression), premature closure (stopping the search once a label fits), availability bias (overweighting recent or memorable cases), confirmation bias. Countermeasures: ask 'what else could this be?', list must-not-miss diagnoses, use checklists and structured scores, and seek a second opinion.

- Sensitivity = TP ÷ (TP + FN); a highly sensitive test, if negative, helps rule out ('SnNOut'). Specificity = TN ÷ (TN + FP); a highly specific test, if positive, helps rule in ('SpPIn').
- PPV = TP ÷ (TP + FP); NPV = TN ÷ (TN + FN). Predictive values depend on prevalence (pre-test probability); sensitivity and specificity do not.
- LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity. Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR.
- Worked example: D-dimer with sensitivity 95% and specificity 50% in 1,000 patients at 10% prevalence gives TP 95, FN 5, TN 450, FP 450. PPV = 95 ÷ 545 ≈ 17%; NPV = 450 ÷ 455 ≈ 99%. LR+ = 0.95 ÷ 0.5 = 1.9; LR− = 0.05 ÷ 0.5 = 0.1. A negative result is useful when probability is low; a positive one proves little.
- Treatment effects: absolute risk reduction (ARR) = control event rate − treated event rate; relative risk reduction (RRR) = ARR ÷ control rate; number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 ÷ ARR. Events falling from 10% to 7.5% give ARR 2.5%, RRR 25%, NNT 40. The same RRR from a baseline of 2% gives ARR 0.5% and NNT 200.

sections.h: Scores and structured responses in UK guidance
sections.body:
- ABCDE (Resuscitation Council UK): assess Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure; treat life-threatening problems as found; reassess, call for help early and hand over with SBAR.
- NEWS2 (RCP, 2017) scores respiration rate, SpO₂, systolic BP, pulse, consciousness (ACVPU, new confusion scores 3) and temperature, plus 2 points for supplemental oxygen. Aggregate 5–6 is the key threshold for an urgent response, 7 or more an emergency response, and a score of 3 in any single parameter prompts urgent ward-based review. SpO₂ Scale 2 (target 88–92%) is used only for confirmed hypercapnic respiratory failure on a clinician's instruction.
- CURB65 (NICE NG250): Confusion, Urea over 7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate 30 or more, low Blood pressure (systolic under 90 or diastolic 60 or less), age 65 or more; 0–1 low, 2 moderate, 3–5 high severity (CRB65, without urea, in primary care). Since 2025: 0–1 usually home with safety-netting, 2 a virtual ward, same-day emergency care, hospital at home or admission, 3 or more inpatient care, with clinical judgement and the person's preferences.
- Suspected PE (NICE NG158): two-level Wells over 4 points, CTPA (with interim anticoagulation if imaging is delayed); 4 or fewer, D-dimer first, and image only if positive.
- AF (NICE NG196): CHA₂DS₂-VASc for stroke risk (offer anticoagulation at 2 or more; consider for men at 1) and ORBIT for bleeding risk, used to address modifiable bleeding factors rather than, by itself, to withhold anticoagulation.
- GMC (2020): share options with their benefits and harms so the patient can decide.

A 30-year-old woman known to have anxiety attends breathless two weeks after knee surgery. Heart rate 112/min, SpO₂ 94% on air. The first clinician labels it a panic attack (anchoring) and stops there (premature closure). A second clinician asks what else could explain it and lists PE as must-not-miss: recent surgery and immobility (Virchow's triad), tachycardia and borderline saturation. The two-level Wells score includes heart rate over 100 (1.5), recent surgery or immobilisation (1.5) and an alternative diagnosis being less likely than PE (3), giving 6: 'PE likely', so NICE recommends CTPA rather than a D-dimer first. Her NEWS2 is raised by the tachycardia and lower saturation, prompting review rather than reassurance.

- Students often say sensitivity depends on prevalence. It does not; predictive values do.
- Students often treat a positive D-dimer as diagnosing PE. D-dimer is non-specific; its value is a negative result in someone with low clinical probability.
- Students often think a large relative risk reduction always means a big benefit. The absolute benefit (and NNT) depends on baseline risk.
- Students often think a high bleeding score means anticoagulation should not be given in AF. NICE uses ORBIT to find and fix modifiable bleeding risks; it is not, by itself, a reason to withhold anticoagulation.
- Students often think ABCDE means completing the whole assessment before treating. Each problem is treated as it is found, then the patient is reassessed.

cards.f: Cardiac output: equation and typical resting value
cards.b: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume; about 5 L/min in a resting adult (approximate).
cards.ex: Remember the two levers: rate and stroke volume (set by preload, afterload and contractility).

cards.f: Which current produces the upstroke of the SA node action potential?
cards.b: L-type Ca²⁺ influx. The slow pacemaker depolarisation before it comes from the funny current (If, HCN channels) and T-type Ca²⁺ channels.
cards.ex: Nodal cells lack a functional fast Na⁺ upstroke; that is why rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers slow them.

cards.f: Why can cardiac muscle not be tetanised?
cards.b: The Ca²⁺ plateau makes the action potential and refractory period last almost as long as the contraction, so a new action potential cannot start until the muscle is relaxing.
cards.ex: Skeletal muscle has a short refractory period, so twitches can summate; cardiac muscle cannot.

cards.f: Why does halving arteriolar radius raise resistance 16-fold?
cards.b: Poiseuille: resistance is proportional to 1/r⁴, so halving r multiplies resistance by 2⁴ = 16.
cards.ex: Radius appears to the fourth power, which is why arterioles are the main site of resistance control.

cards.f: A student stands up quickly and feels light-headed for a few seconds before recovering. What reflex restored her blood pressure?
cards.b: Blood pooled in the legs, so baroreceptor firing fell; the brainstem raised sympathetic and cut vagal outflow, increasing heart rate, contractility and vascular tone.
cards.ex: Less stretch → less baroreceptor firing → more sympathetic drive.

cards.f: Why does a low serum albumin cause oedema?
cards.b: Albumin provides most plasma oncotic pressure. When it falls, less fluid is held in the capillaries, so filtration exceeds lymphatic return.
cards.ex: Starling forces: hydrostatic out, oncotic in.

cards.f: How does surfactant keep small alveoli open?
cards.b: It lowers surface tension, more so in small alveoli. By Laplace (P = 2T/r) this stops small alveoli emptying into large ones and raises compliance.
cards.ex: Without surfactant, small radius means a high collapsing pressure.

cards.f: Bohr effect vs Haldane effect
cards.b: Bohr: raised CO₂/H⁺ lowers haemoglobin’s O₂ affinity (right shift), aiding O₂ unloading in tissues. Haldane: deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO₂, aiding CO₂ loading in tissues and release in the lungs.
cards.ex: Bohr is about O₂ carriage changed by CO₂; Haldane is about CO₂ carriage changed by O₂.

cards.f: Where in the upright lung is the V/Q ratio highest, and why?
cards.b: At the apex. Ventilation and perfusion both fall towards the apex, but perfusion falls more because of gravity, so V/Q is high there and low at the base.
cards.ex: Perfusion is the more gravity-dependent of the two.

cards.f: A man with coronary disease develops angina during a fast arrhythmia. Why does tachycardia provoke ischaemia?
cards.b: Left ventricular coronary flow occurs mainly in diastole; a fast rate shortens diastole (less supply) while raising myocardial oxygen demand.
cards.ex: Supply falls and demand rises at the same time.

cards.f: Central vs peripheral chemoreceptors
cards.b: Central (medulla) respond to CSF H⁺ from arterial CO₂ and give most resting drive. Peripheral (carotid and aortic bodies) respond mainly to low PaO₂ (strongly below about 8 kPa) and to H⁺.
cards.ex: CO₂ is the minute-to-minute signal; hypoxia matters when PaO₂ is clearly low.

cards.f: Type I vs type II pneumocytes
cards.b: Type I: thin cells forming most of the gas-exchange surface. Type II: secrete surfactant and act as progenitors for type I cells.
cards.ex: Type II cells are the surfactant factories.

cards.f: Virchow's triad
cards.b: Stasis of blood flow, hypercoagulability, and vessel wall (endothelial) injury.
cards.ex: Every VTE risk factor works through at least one of these three.

cards.f: Pack-years: formula
cards.b: Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked.
cards.ex: One pack is 20 cigarettes; 40 a day for 10 years = 20 pack-years.

cards.f: How does a fatty streak form?
cards.b: Oxidised LDL in the intima is taken up by macrophages derived from monocytes; these lipid-laden foam cells make the fatty streak, the earliest visible lesion.
cards.ex: Endothelial dysfunction → LDL entry and oxidation → monocytes → foam cells.

cards.f: Why is a thin-capped plaque dangerous even if it narrows the artery only slightly?
cards.b: A thin fibrous cap over a large lipid core with many inflammatory cells is prone to rupture; exposed core triggers thrombosis, which can occlude the artery suddenly.
cards.ex: Rupture risk depends on plaque composition, not degree of stenosis.

cards.f: Centriacinar vs panacinar emphysema
cards.b: Centriacinar: central respiratory bronchioles, upper zones, typical of smoking. Panacinar: whole acinus, lower zones, typical of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
cards.ex: Basal panacinar emphysema in a non-smoker or young person should prompt AAT testing.

cards.f: How does emphysema reduce expiratory airflow when it is a disease of the alveoli?
cards.b: Destroyed alveolar walls lose elastic recoil and the radial traction that holds small airways open, so the airways collapse on expiration and air is trapped.
cards.ex: Less recoil to drive air out, and floppy airways that close early.

cards.f: Why does atrial fibrillation cause stroke?
cards.b: Ineffective atrial contraction lets blood stagnate, especially in the left atrial appendage (stasis in Virchow’s triad); thrombus forms and can embolise to the brain.
cards.ex: Stasis is the key arm of the triad here.

cards.f: A 30-year-old has total cholesterol 9 mmol/L, tendon xanthomata and a father with a myocardial infarction at 45. Should QRISK3 be used to decide on statin treatment?
cards.b: No. Suspected familial hypercholesterolaemia already means high risk; NICE says not to use a risk tool in FH. Refer for specialist assessment and test relatives.
cards.ex: Risk scores underestimate risk in inherited lipid disorders.

cards.f: Modifiable vs non-modifiable cardiovascular risk factors (two of each)
cards.b: Modifiable: smoking, hypertension, raised LDL/non-HDL, diabetes, obesity, inactivity. Non-modifiable: age, male sex, family history of premature CVD, ethnicity.
cards.ex: Modifiable = something treatment or behaviour can change.

cards.f: A QRISK3 score of 14% in a 58-year-old without CVD: what does it mean?
cards.b: About 14 in 100 people like them would have a heart attack or stroke in the next 10 years. NICE offers a statin at 10% or more, after discussing lifestyle change.
cards.ex: The score is a population estimate, used for shared decisions.

cards.f: Why is familial hypercholesterolaemia usually seen in every generation?
cards.b: It is usually autosomal dominant: one faulty copy of LDLR, APOB or PCSK9 is enough, and each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting it.
cards.ex: Dominant inheritance → vertical transmission.

cards.f: Chronic bronchitis vs emphysema: how is each defined?
cards.b: Chronic bronchitis is clinical: productive cough on most days for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years. Emphysema is structural: permanent enlargement of air spaces with destruction of alveolar walls.
cards.ex: One is defined by symptoms, the other by pathology; many patients with COPD have both.

cards.f: ECG timing at 25 mm/s
cards.b: Small square 0.04 s; large square 0.2 s. Regular rate = 300 ÷ large squares between R waves (or 1,500 ÷ small squares).
cards.ex: Five small squares make one large square.

cards.f: Irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves, 15 QRS complexes on a 10-second strip. Interpret.
cards.b: Atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 90/min (15 × 6).
cards.ex: Irregular rhythm: count complexes in 10 s and multiply by 6.

cards.f: ST elevation in II, III and aVF with ST depression in aVL. Which territory and usual artery?
cards.b: Inferior STEMI, usually right coronary artery (sometimes circumflex). aVL shows the reciprocal change.
cards.ex: II, III, aVF look at the inferior wall.

cards.f: Obstructive vs restrictive spirometry
cards.b: Obstructive: FEV₁/FVC below 0.7 (FEV₁ reduced more than FVC). Restrictive: FVC reduced with a normal or high ratio.
cards.ex: Read the ratio first, then the volumes.

cards.f: Type 1 vs type 2 respiratory failure
cards.b: Both have PaO₂ below 8 kPa. Type 1: PaCO₂ normal or low (V/Q mismatch). Type 2: PaCO₂ raised, above about 6.0 kPa (alveolar hypoventilation).
cards.ex: The CO₂ tells you whether ventilation is failing.

cards.f: Percussion stony dull, absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance at the right base; trachea central. Most likely?
cards.b: Right pleural effusion. Fluid separates lung from chest wall, so it is very dull and transmits sound poorly.
cards.ex: Consolidation is dull but has bronchial breathing and increased resonance.

cards.f: Why does consolidation cause bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance?
cards.b: Fluid-filled alveoli around patent airways conduct sound from the large airways to the chest wall better than air-filled lung does.
cards.ex: Solid tissue transmits sound well; fluid in the pleural space or air does not.

cards.f: Why can a raised A–a gradient separate PE from opioid-induced hypoventilation?
cards.b: Pure hypoventilation lowers PAO₂ and PaO₂ together (normal gradient). PE causes V/Q mismatch, so PaO₂ falls far below PAO₂ (raised gradient).
cards.ex: PAO₂ ≈ 20 − PaCO₂/0.8 kPa on air.

cards.f: PR interval of 7 small squares, constant, every P conducted. Interpret.
cards.b: PR = 0.28 s: first-degree AV block (delay in the AV node).
cards.ex: Above 0.20 s (5 small squares) is prolonged.

cards.f: Why does pulse oximetry read normally in carbon monoxide poisoning?
cards.b: Carboxyhaemoglobin absorbs light similarly to oxyhaemoglobin, so standard oximeters count it as oxygenated.
cards.ex: Use co-oximetry on a blood gas to measure COHb.

cards.f: Post-bronchodilator FEV₁ 1.8 L, FVC 3.2 L in a 62-year-old smoker with exertional breathlessness. Interpret.
cards.b: Ratio 1.8 ÷ 3.2 ≈ 0.56, below 0.7: persistent airflow obstruction, consistent with COPD in this context.
cards.ex: NICE NG115 uses post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC below 0.7.

cards.f: Tension pneumothorax vs lobar collapse: tracheal position
cards.b: Tension pneumothorax pushes the trachea away from the affected side; lobar collapse pulls it towards the affected side.
cards.ex: Push = extra volume (air/fluid); pull = lost volume.

cards.f: Why does an ACE inhibitor cause dry cough?
cards.b: ACE also breaks down bradykinin; inhibiting it lets bradykinin (and related mediators) build up in the airway, causing cough. ARBs do not do this.
cards.ex: ACE = kininase II.

cards.f: Why does aspirin's antiplatelet effect last days after the drug has gone?
cards.b: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1, and platelets have no nucleus to make new enzyme, so the effect lasts the platelet’s lifespan (about 7–10 days, approximate).
cards.ex: Recovery needs new platelets.

cards.f: Antiplatelet vs anticoagulant
cards.b: Antiplatelets (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors) stop platelet activation (arterial, platelet-rich clots). Anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs, heparins) inhibit clotting factors (venous clots, AF).
cards.ex: Platelets vs clotting cascade.

cards.f: Why is verapamil dangerous with a β-blocker?
cards.b: Both slow the SA and AV nodes and reduce contractility, so together they can cause severe bradycardia, AV block, hypotension and heart failure.
cards.ex: Additive negative chronotropic and inotropic effects.

cards.f: How does hypokalaemia increase digoxin toxicity?
cards.b: Digoxin and K⁺ compete for the same site on Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; with less K⁺, digoxin binds more, so its effect and toxicity rise.
cards.ex: Watch potassium when diuretics are increased.

cards.f: How does GTN relieve angina?
cards.b: It releases nitric oxide, raising cGMP in vascular smooth muscle; venodilation lowers preload and wall stress, reducing myocardial oxygen demand (plus some coronary dilation).
cards.ex: Mainly a venodilator.

cards.f: Statins: target and effect on LDL receptors
cards.b: Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase (rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis); hepatocytes upregulate LDL receptors and clear more LDL from blood.
cards.ex: Less intracellular cholesterol → more LDL receptors.

cards.f: A 60-year-old white man with hypertension, no diabetes. Step 1 drug class under NICE NG136?
cards.b: A calcium-channel blocker, because he is 55 or over and does not have type 2 diabetes.
cards.ex: Under 55 (not Black African/African-Caribbean origin) or type 2 diabetes → ACE inhibitor or ARB.

cards.f: Dihydropyridine vs rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers
cards.b: Dihydropyridines (amlodipine) mainly dilate arterioles. Rate-limiting agents (verapamil, diltiazem) also slow SA and AV nodal conduction and reduce contractility.
cards.ex: Only the rate-limiting ones are used for rate control.

cards.f: Why do selected β-blockers improve survival in HFrEF despite lowering contractility?
cards.b: Chronic sympathetic activation is toxic (tachycardia, arrhythmias, remodelling, myocyte death). Blocking it, introduced gradually, improves remodelling and survival.
cards.ex: Short-term negative inotropy, long-term benefit.

cards.f: Four HFrEF medicine classes NICE recommends offering
cards.b: ACE inhibitor (or ARNI/ARB as appropriate), β-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and SGLT2 inhibitor.
cards.ex: Diuretics are for congestion, not survival.

cards.f: A newly diagnosed 25-year-old with mild asthma, no severe exacerbation. First treatment under BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024?
cards.b: As-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol (AIR therapy), not a SABA alone.
cards.ex: Highly symptomatic or severe exacerbation at presentation → MART.

cards.f: Sensitivity and specificity: formulae
cards.b: Sensitivity = TP ÷ (TP + FN). Specificity = TN ÷ (TN + FP).
cards.ex: Sensitivity is among people WITH disease; specificity among those WITHOUT.

cards.f: Sensitivity vs positive predictive value
cards.b: Sensitivity: proportion of diseased people who test positive (independent of prevalence). PPV: proportion of positive tests that are true (rises with prevalence).
cards.ex: PPV changes when the same test is used in a different population.

cards.f: Event rate falls from 10% to 7.5% on treatment. ARR, RRR and NNT?
cards.ex: NNT = 1 ÷ ARR (as a proportion).

cards.f: Why is D-dimer used only to rule out PE in low-probability patients?
cards.b: It is sensitive but non-specific: a negative result in a low-probability patient makes PE very unlikely (high NPV), but many conditions raise it, so a positive result proves little.
cards.ex: SnNOut: sensitive test, negative result, rules out.

cards.f: A ward patient has NEWS2 aggregate 7. What response does RCP guidance indicate?
cards.b: High clinical risk: an emergency response, with a team that includes critical-care skills.
cards.ex: 5–6 urgent response; 7 or more emergency response.

cards.f: Pneumonia: aged 72, new confusion, urea 9 mmol/L, RR 24, BP 118/70. CURB65?
cards.b: 3 (confusion, urea over 7, age 65 or more): high severity; NICE NG250 indicates inpatient care with critical care review if appropriate.
cards.ex: RR must be 30 or more to score.

cards.f: A 78-year-old man with AF, treated hypertension and a TIA last year. CHA₂DS₂-VASc?
cards.b: Age 75 or over (2) + hypertension (1) + TIA (2) = 5.
cards.ex: Age 75+ and stroke/TIA each score 2.

cards.f: Anchoring vs premature closure
cards.b: Anchoring: fixing on early information and failing to adjust. Premature closure: accepting a diagnosis before it is verified and stopping the search.
cards.ex: Countermeasure for both: deliberately ask "what else could this be?"

cards.f: Two-level Wells score 3 in suspected PE. Next step under NICE NG158?
cards.b: PE unlikely: offer a D-dimer; image (CTPA) only if positive.
cards.ex: Over 4 = PE likely → CTPA.

cards.f: How do likelihood ratios change probability?
cards.b: Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR. LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity.
cards.ex: Convert probability to odds, multiply, then convert back.

cards.f: Six dangerous causes of chest pain to exclude
cards.b: Acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, oesophageal rupture.
cards.ex: Order differentials by danger as well as likelihood.

cards.f: Why does a test’s PPV fall when used for screening a low-risk population?
cards.b: With low prevalence, even a small false-positive rate among the many disease-free people outnumbers the true positives.
cards.ex: PPV depends on prevalence.

questions.q: Which ionic current is mainly responsible for the upstroke (phase 0) of the sinoatrial node action potential?
options: Influx of Na⁺ through fast voltage-gated sodium channels
The funny current (If) through HCN channels
Influx of Ca²⁺ through L-type calcium channels
Efflux of K⁺ through delayed rectifier channels
questions.why: SA node cells have a slow upstroke carried by L-type Ca²⁺ channels once the pacemaker potential (funny current then T-type Ca²⁺) reaches threshold. This is why nodal tissue is slowed by rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers.
optWhy: Fast Na⁺ channels carry phase 0 in atrial and ventricular myocytes, not in nodal cells.
The funny current drives the slow pacemaker depolarisation before threshold, not the upstroke itself.
Correct: in nodal cells the upstroke is carried by L-type Ca²⁺ channels, so it is slower than in ventricular muscle.
K⁺ efflux repolarises the cell; it does not depolarise it.
questions.clue: 'Upstroke (phase 0)' and 'sinoatrial node'.
questions.concept: Ionic basis of the nodal action potential differs from that of ventricular myocytes.

followUp.q: A drug that blocks HCN channels in the SA node is given to a patient in sinus rhythm. What is the main expected effect?
options: Weaker ventricular contraction because less Ca²⁺ enters myocytes
A longer QRS complex because ventricular conduction slows
Slower heart rate because the pacemaker potential rises more slowly
Faster heart rate because repolarisation is shortened
followUp.why: HCN channels carry the funny current that sets the slope of the pacemaker potential; blocking it flattens the slope and slows the rate (ivabradine works this way). It does not act on ventricular Ca²⁺ entry or conduction, so contractility and QRS width are unchanged.

questions.q: An arteriole constricts so that its radius halves, while its length and blood viscosity stay the same. By roughly how much does its resistance to flow change?
questions.why: Poiseuille's relationship gives resistance = 8ηL ÷ πr⁴. With η and L unchanged, halving the radius multiplies resistance by 2⁴ = 16. This fourth-power relationship is why small changes in arteriolar tone control blood pressure and regional flow.
optWhy: Doubling would apply if resistance were proportional to 1/r.
Correct: resistance ∝ 1/r⁴, so (1/0.5)⁴ = 16.
A 4-fold rise would apply if resistance depended on 1/r² (cross-sectional area alone).
Eight-fold would apply to 1/r³; the 8 in Poiseuille’s equation is a constant, not the answer.
Narrowing a vessel increases resistance; it does not reduce it.
questions.clue: 'Radius halves' while 'length and viscosity stay the same'.
questions.concept: Poiseuille's law: resistance is inversely proportional to radius to the fourth power.

followUp.q: In exercising muscle, local metabolites dilate an arteriole so its radius increases by 20%. Roughly what happens to its resistance?
options: It falls to about half of the original
It falls to about 80% of the original
followUp.why: New resistance = 1 ÷ 1.2⁴ ≈ 1 ÷ 2.07 ≈ 0.48 of the original, so it roughly halves. Falling by 20% treats resistance as proportional to radius rather than to its fourth power; dilation cannot raise resistance.

questions.q: A 21-year-old stands up quickly after lying on the sofa. For a few seconds she feels light-headed, then recovers. Which change best explains her recovery?
options: Increased baroreceptor firing, increasing vagal outflow to the SA node
Stimulation of central chemoreceptors by a rise in arterial CO₂
Release of atrial natriuretic peptide from stretched atria
Hypoxic vasoconstriction of skeletal muscle arterioles
Reduced carotid sinus and aortic arch firing, increasing sympathetic and reducing vagal outflow
questions.why: Standing pools blood in the legs, so venous return, stroke volume and arterial pressure briefly fall. Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus (IX) and aortic arch (X) fire less, and the brainstem raises sympathetic and lowers vagal outflow within seconds. Heart rate, contractility and vascular tone rise and pressure recovers.
optWhy: Increased firing happens when pressure rises; it would slow the heart and lower pressure further.
Standing does not raise arterial CO₂; chemoreceptors control ventilation rather than this rapid pressure correction.
ANP is released when the atria are stretched by volume overload; on standing, venous return falls.
Systemic arterioles dilate, not constrict, in response to local hypoxia, and that response is not what restores pressure here.
Correct: lower pressure means less stretch and less baroreceptor firing, which raises heart rate, contractility and vascular tone.
questions.clue: Brief light-headedness on standing that resolves within seconds.
questions.concept: The baroreceptor reflex corrects short-term changes in arterial pressure.

followUp.q: During carotid sinus massage the heart rate of a patient in sinus rhythm slows. What explains this?
options: Reduced baroreceptor firing raising sympathetic outflow
Direct compression of the SA node artery
Stimulation of the carotid body chemoreceptors by hypoxia
Increased baroreceptor firing raising vagal outflow
followUp.why: Pressure on the carotid sinus mimics a rise in blood pressure, so baroreceptor firing increases and vagal outflow to the SA and AV nodes rises, slowing the heart. Reduced firing would speed it up; the SA node artery lies in the heart, not the neck; the carotid body is a chemoreceptor, not a stretch receptor.

questions.q: During a hard rowing session, the temperature, PCO₂ and H⁺ concentration of the blood in a working muscle all rise. What is the effect on oxygen delivery?
options: The oxygen–haemoglobin curve shifts right, so more O₂ is released at a given PO₂
The curve shifts left, so haemoglobin holds O₂ more tightly
The curve becomes hyperbolic, so cooperative binding is lost
Haemoglobin carries less CO₂ because it is deoxygenated
Arterial O₂ saturation falls well below 90% in a healthy athlete
questions.why: Raised CO₂, H⁺ and temperature lower haemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen (the Bohr effect and a temperature effect), shifting the dissociation curve to the right. At the low PO₂ in working muscle, more oxygen is released, matching delivery to demand.
optWhy: Correct: the Bohr effect plus heat shift the curve right, lowering affinity where O₂ is needed.
A left shift happens with lower temperature, CO₂, H⁺ or 2,3-BPG (or with fetal haemoglobin), not in exercising muscle.
The sigmoid shape reflects cooperative binding and is kept; only the position shifts.
The Haldane effect is the reverse: deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO₂.
In healthy people arterial saturation stays high in exercise; the change is in unloading at the tissues.
questions.clue: Temperature, PCO₂ and H⁺ 'all rise' in working muscle.
questions.concept: Factors shifting the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve.

followUp.q: Blood stored for several weeks has low 2,3-BPG. Soon after a large transfusion of it, how is oxygen unloading affected?
options: It is reduced, because the curve is shifted left
It is increased, because the curve is shifted right
It is unchanged, because 2,3-BPG affects only CO₂ carriage
It is reduced, because haemoglobin can no longer bind oxygen
followUp.why: 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhaemoglobin and lowers its O₂ affinity. With less of it, the curve shifts left and haemoglobin gives up oxygen less readily until red cells regenerate 2,3-BPG. Haemoglobin still binds oxygen normally; it simply holds it more tightly.

questions.q: A patient breathes with a tidal volume of 400 mL at 20 breaths per minute. Anatomical dead space is 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
questions.why: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × respiratory rate = (400 − 150) × 20 = 5,000 mL/min = 5.0 L/min. Only the part of each breath that passes the conducting airways takes part in gas exchange.
optWhy: This is minute ventilation (400 × 20); dead space has not been subtracted.
This is dead-space ventilation (150 × 20).
This adds dead space to tidal volume ((400 + 150) × 20).
This uses the rate as 10 rather than 20 ((400 − 150) × 10).
questions.clue: Tidal volume 400 mL, rate 20/min and dead space 150 mL are all given.
questions.concept: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × rate.

followUp.q: At rest, oxygen consumption is 250 mL/min, arterial O₂ content 200 mL/L and mixed venous O₂ content 150 mL/L. What is the cardiac output by the Fick principle?
followUp.why: Cardiac output = VO₂ ÷ (CaO₂ − CvO₂) = 250 ÷ (200 − 150) = 250 ÷ 50 = 5 L/min. Dividing by the arterial content alone (250 ÷ 200) gives 1.25; inverting the ratio gives 0.2; dividing by 20 instead of 50 gives 12.5.

questions.q: At rest, a patient’s oxygen consumption is 300 mL/min, arterial O₂ content is 200 mL/L and mixed venous O₂ content is 150 mL/L. Calculate the cardiac output using the Fick principle, then explain what happens to mixed venous O₂ content if cardiac output falls with oxygen consumption unchanged.
markScheme: States Fick: cardiac output = VO₂ ÷ (CaO₂ − CvO₂)
Correct calculation: 300 ÷ 50 = 6 L/min with units
If cardiac output falls, each litre of blood spends longer in the tissues and more O₂ is extracted
Arteriovenous O₂ difference widens, so mixed venous O₂ content (and saturation) falls
Links to clinical use: a low mixed venous saturation suggests inadequate delivery (e.g. shock or heart failure)
questions.modelAnswer: The Fick principle states that oxygen taken up by the body equals blood flow multiplied by the arteriovenous difference in oxygen content. So cardiac output = VO₂ ÷ (CaO₂ − CvO₂) = 300 mL/min ÷ (200 − 150) mL/L = 300 ÷ 50 = 6 L/min. If cardiac output falls while the tissues still need 300 mL of oxygen each minute, the tissues must remove more oxygen from each litre of blood. The arteriovenous difference widens and mixed venous O₂ content falls (for example, at an output of 4 L/min the difference must be 75 mL/L, giving a CvO₂ of 125 mL/L). A low mixed venous saturation is therefore a sign that delivery is not keeping up with demand, as in shock or severe heart failure.
questions.concept: Fick principle: cardiac output = VO₂ ÷ arteriovenous O₂ difference.

questions.q: A 25-year-old motorcyclist is brought to the emergency department after a collision, with a fractured femur and an estimated blood loss of 1.5 litres. Heart rate 126/min, blood pressure 98/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, cool peripheries, anxious. Explain, with reference to relevant equations and reflexes, how his cardiovascular system is responding, why his blood pressure is relatively preserved, and what would happen if bleeding continued.
markScheme: Blood loss reduces venous return and preload, so stroke volume falls (Frank–Starling); CO = HR × SV
Baroreceptors (carotid sinus IX, aortic arch X) fire less; NTS-mediated rise in sympathetic and fall in vagal outflow
Tachycardia and raised contractility partly restore CO; arteriolar constriction raises TPR (MAP ≈ CO × TPR), venoconstriction mobilises venous blood
Narrow pulse pressure (20 mmHg here) reflects low stroke volume with high TPR; cool peripheries from skin vasoconstriction
Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls, so interstitial fluid moves into plasma (Starling forces)
Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and ADH conserve salt and water over hours; thirst
Continued loss: compensation fails, MAP and organ perfusion fall, anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis; hypotension is a late sign
Clear structure, correct use of equations, values described as approximate
questions.modelAnswer:
He has lost roughly a third of an adult blood volume (approximate), and his findings show compensation under strain.

Preload and stroke volume. Losing blood reduces venous return, so ventricular filling (preload) falls. By the Frank–Starling mechanism a less-stretched ventricle ejects a smaller stroke volume. Because cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, output would fall unless something else changed.

Baroreceptor reflex. Lower arterial pressure reduces stretch of the carotid sinus (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic arch (vagus) baroreceptors. The nucleus tractus solitarius responds by increasing sympathetic and reducing vagal outflow. Heart rate rises (126/min) and β1 stimulation increases contractility, partly restoring cardiac output. α-adrenergic constriction of arterioles in skin, gut and kidney raises total peripheral resistance, and venoconstriction pushes blood from the veins back to the heart. Since mean arterial pressure ≈ cardiac output × TPR, the rise in TPR holds MAP up despite the low output. His diastolic pressure of 78 mmHg is relatively high, and his pulse pressure is only 20 mmHg: the small stroke volume lowers systolic pressure while the high resistance keeps diastolic pressure up. His cool peripheries reflect skin vasoconstriction, and tachypnoea and anxiety reflect sympathetic activation and early tissue hypoperfusion.

Fluid shifts and hormones. Arteriolar constriction lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure, so Starling forces favour movement of interstitial fluid into the plasma, partly refilling the circulation. Reduced renal perfusion and sympathetic activity release renin; angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone, which conserves sodium and water. ADH is released and thirst increases. These slower mechanisms work over hours.

If bleeding continues. Compensation has limits. As loss increases, tachycardia shortens diastolic filling, cardiac output falls further and MAP drops. Organ perfusion fails: urine output falls, confusion develops and cells switch to anaerobic metabolism, producing lactic acidosis. Hypotension is therefore a late sign, and a normal-looking blood pressure must not reassure when the heart rate is rising and the pulse pressure is narrow.
questions.concept: Integrated cardiovascular response to haemorrhage (CO = HR × SV; MAP ≈ CO × TPR; baroreflex; Starling forces).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the components of Virchow's triad?
questions.why: Virchow's triad describes the three conditions that favour thrombosis: stasis, hypercoagulability and vessel wall injury. Raised blood pressure promotes atherosclerosis but is not part of the triad.
optWhy: Stasis is a component (e.g. immobility, AF).
Hypercoagulability is a component (e.g. cancer, pregnancy, thrombophilia).
Vessel wall injury is a component (e.g. surgery, central lines).
Correct: hypertension is a risk factor for arterial disease, not a component of the triad for thrombosis.
questions.clue: 'NOT one of the components'.
questions.concept: The three components of Virchow's triad.

followUp.q: A woman develops a deep vein thrombosis two weeks after a long-haul flight while taking an oestrogen-containing contraceptive pill. Which two arms of the triad are most clearly involved?
followUp.why: Prolonged sitting causes venous stasis, and oestrogen increases clotting factor production (hypercoagulability). There is no clear vessel wall injury here, and hypertension is not a component of the triad.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman who has never smoked has progressive breathlessness. CT shows emphysema that is panacinar and predominantly in the lower lobes. Her brother had liver disease in his thirties. Which underlying condition is most likely?
options: Smoking-related centriacinar emphysema from passive smoking
questions.why: Panacinar, lower-zone emphysema in a never-smoker, with a family history of liver disease, points to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Without enough antiprotease, neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar walls. NICE NG115 advises testing alpha-1 antitrypsin when COPD starts early, with minimal smoking history, or with a family history.
optWhy: Cystic fibrosis mainly causes bronchiectasis with infection, usually diagnosed in childhood, not basal panacinar emphysema.
Asthma causes variable obstruction from airway inflammation, not destruction of alveolar walls.
Correct: lack of antiprotease leaves alveolar walls unprotected (basal panacinar emphysema); misfolded protein can also damage the liver.
Smoking-related emphysema is typically centriacinar and upper-zone.
FH causes very high LDL and premature atherosclerosis, not emphysema.
questions.clue: 'Never smoked', 'panacinar', 'lower lobes' and a brother with liver disease.
questions.concept: Protease–antiprotease imbalance and the pattern of emphysema.

followUp.q: A 70-year-old who has smoked 50 pack-years has emphysema on CT. Where would the changes typically be most marked?
followUp.why: Smoking-related emphysema is typically centriacinar (around the respiratory bronchioles) and worst in the upper zones. Lower-zone panacinar change suggests alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; bronchiectasis is a different disease of dilated airways.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man collapses with chest pain and dies. At post-mortem a coronary artery contains thrombus over a plaque that had narrowed the lumen by only about 40%. Which plaque feature most likely explains the event?
options: A thick, heavily calcified fibrous cap
A thin fibrous cap over a large lipid-rich core with many macrophages
A severe fixed stenosis limiting flow on exertion
A fatty streak with no fibrous cap
Dense smooth muscle with little lipid
questions.why: Acute coronary syndromes usually follow rupture or erosion of a vulnerable plaque. A thin fibrous cap over a large lipid core, weakened by macrophage enzymes, can tear; exposed core material triggers thrombosis. The degree of narrowing is a poor guide to rupture risk.
optWhy: A thick cap makes a plaque more stable, not less.
Correct: thin-capped, lipid-rich, inflamed plaques are vulnerable to rupture and thrombosis.
The lesion was only 40% stenotic; acute events often arise from non-flow-limiting plaques.
Fatty streaks are early lesions without a cap and do not cause thrombosis like this.
Plaques rich in smooth muscle and collagen with little lipid are stable.
questions.clue: Thrombus over a plaque narrowing the lumen 'only about 40%'.
questions.concept: Plaque vulnerability depends on composition, not stenosis.

followUp.q: A man has chest tightness only when walking uphill, relieved within minutes by rest. Angiography shows a smooth, thick-capped plaque narrowing an artery by 80%. What is the mechanism of his symptoms?
options: Fixed narrowing limits flow when myocardial oxygen demand rises
Repeated plaque rupture with transient thrombosis
followUp.why: Stable angina reflects a fixed stenosis: at rest flow is enough, but on exertion demand outstrips supply. Plaque rupture causes acute coronary syndromes; spasm causes pain at rest; atrial emboli cause stroke or limb ischaemia rather than exertional angina.

questions.q: A patient has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 40 years. How many pack-years is this?
questions.why: Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked = (30 ÷ 20) × 40 = 60. NICE NG115 recommends recording pack-years for everyone with COPD.
optWhy: This uses cigarettes per day as packs per day.
This counts years only, as if one pack a day.
This multiplies cigarettes by years without dividing by 20.
This inverts the ratio ((20 ÷ 30) × 40).
questions.clue: 30 cigarettes a day for 40 years.
questions.concept: Calculating pack-years.

followUp.q: A woman smoked 10 cigarettes a day for 24 years. How many pack-years?
followUp.why: (10 ÷ 20) × 24 = 0.5 × 24 = 12 pack-years. 24 counts years only; 240 multiplies cigarettes by years; 48 doubles instead of halving.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman without cardiovascular disease, diabetes or kidney disease has a 10-year QRISK3 score of 12% after lifestyle advice. According to NICE NG238, what is the most appropriate approach to statin treatment?
options: Offer a statin for primary prevention, as part of a shared decision
Do not offer a statin, because her risk is below 20%
Use QRISK3 again only after she reaches 65
Offer a statin only if her total cholesterol is above 7.5 mmol/L
Refer for genetic testing for familial hypercholesterolaemia
questions.why: NICE NG238 recommends offering a statin for primary prevention to people with a 10-year QRISK3 risk of 10% or more, after discussing lifestyle change and the person’s preferences. Checked October 2026; check the current guideline.
optWhy: Correct: NICE offers a statin when the 10-year QRISK3 risk is 10% or more.
The threshold is 10%, not 20% (20% was an older threshold).
QRISK3 is used from age 25 to 84; there is no reason to wait.
The decision in primary prevention rests on overall risk, not on a cholesterol cut-off.
Nothing here suggests FH (no very high cholesterol, xanthomata or family history).
questions.clue: QRISK3 '12%' in someone without CVD, diabetes or CKD.
questions.concept: NICE threshold for offering a statin in primary prevention.

followUp.q: A 40-year-old has type 1 diabetes. Should QRISK3 be used to decide on statin treatment?
options: Yes; QRISK3 is validated for everyone aged 25 to 84
No; NICE says not to use a risk tool for people with type 1 diabetes, who are already at increased risk
Yes, but only if he also smokes
No; statins are never used in type 1 diabetes
followUp.why: NICE NG238 lists type 1 diabetes, CKD (eGFR below 60 and/or albuminuria) and FH as groups in whom a risk tool should not be used because they are already at increased risk; statins are offered to adults with type 1 diabetes who meet set criteria.

questions.q: Explain how cigarette smoking leads to emphysema, and why this reduces expiratory airflow even though emphysema is a disease of the alveoli.
markScheme: Smoke recruits neutrophils and macrophages, which release proteases (e.g. elastase); oxidants inactivate antiproteases such as alpha-1 antitrypsin
Protease–antiprotease imbalance destroys alveolar walls: fewer, larger air spaces, typically centriacinar and upper-zone in smokers
Loss of elastic tissue reduces lung recoil, the driving pressure for passive expiration
