Loss of alveolar attachments removes radial traction, so small airways collapse during expiration (dynamic airway collapse, air trapping)
Result: reduced FEV₁ and FEV₁/FVC, hyperinflation; destruction of capillary bed also lowers TLCO
questions.modelAnswer: Cigarette smoke irritates the airways and recruits neutrophils and macrophages, which release proteases such as neutrophil elastase. Oxidants in smoke also inactivate antiproteases, especially alpha-1 antitrypsin. The balance tips towards proteolysis, and the walls of the alveoli are destroyed, leaving fewer, larger air spaces; in smokers this is typically centriacinar and worst in the upper zones. Although the damage is to alveoli, airflow suffers for two reasons. First, alveolar walls contain elastic tissue that provides the recoil driving quiet expiration; with less recoil, there is less pressure pushing air out. Second, the alveolar walls attached to small airways normally pull them open (radial traction). When these attachments are lost, small airways collapse during expiration, trapping air behind them. The result is obstruction (low FEV₁ and FEV₁/FVC), hyperinflation and, because the capillary bed is also destroyed, a low gas transfer factor.
questions.concept: Protease–antiprotease imbalance; loss of recoil and radial traction causes expiratory airflow limitation.

questions.q: "Most cases of chronic lung disease and heart disease in the UK are preventable." Discuss this statement with reference to COPD, asthma, coronary heart disease and lung cancer. Distinguish causes from triggers, and modifiable from non-modifiable risk factors.
markScheme: Defines causes (produce disease) vs triggers (provoke episodes in existing disease) and modifiable vs non-modifiable factors
COPD: smoking the main cause in the UK, plus occupational dusts and fumes; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency non-modifiable; stopping smoking slows decline
Asthma: genetic and atopic predisposition largely not preventable; triggers (allergens, viruses, smoke, NSAIDs, β-blockers) modifiable; preventing attacks differs from preventing disease
Coronary heart disease: smoking, hypertension, LDL/non-HDL, diabetes, obesity, inactivity modifiable; age, sex, family history, FH not modifiable (but FH is treatable)
Lung cancer: smoking the main cause; radon, asbestos, passive smoking, air pollution; some cases in never-smokers
Prevention levels: primary (smoking cessation, BP and lipid control via QRISK3-guided statins), secondary (screening such as AAA), tertiary
Balanced conclusion: much but not all disease is preventable; inequalities and structural determinants matter
Accurate, specific UK examples; no unsupported statistics
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement is largely true for some diseases and much less so for others, and the distinction between causes and triggers helps to judge it.

Definitions. A cause produces disease in someone who would not otherwise have it; a trigger provokes an episode in someone who already has the disease. Modifiable risk factors can be changed by behaviour, treatment or policy; non-modifiable ones (age, sex, genes, family history) cannot.

COPD. In the UK, cigarette smoking is the main cause: proteases released by inflammatory cells overwhelm antiproteases and destroy alveolar walls. Occupational dusts and fumes add to risk. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a non-modifiable cause, though smoking greatly accelerates damage in affected people. Because most cases follow smoking, COPD is largely preventable, and stopping smoking slows the loss of lung function in people who already have it.

Asthma. Here the statement fits poorly. Asthma reflects genetic and atopic predisposition with Th2-driven airway inflammation, and we cannot reliably prevent it developing. What can be modified are triggers (allergens, viral infections, tobacco smoke, cold air, and in some people NSAIDs or β-blockers) and treatment: regular anti-inflammatory therapy prevents many attacks. So asthma attacks are often preventable, but asthma itself mostly is not.

Coronary heart disease. Atherosclerosis is driven by smoking, hypertension, raised LDL or non-HDL cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, inactivity and diet, all modifiable. Age, male sex, ethnicity and family history are not. Familial hypercholesterolaemia is a non-modifiable genetic cause, but its consequences are largely preventable by early diagnosis, lipid-lowering treatment and testing relatives. NICE uses QRISK3 to target statins at people with a 10-year risk of 10% or more.

Lung cancer. Smoking is the main cause, with passive smoking, radon, asbestos and air pollution also contributing. A substantial minority of cases occur in never-smokers, so not all lung cancer is preventable, but most is.

Levels of prevention. Primary prevention removes causes (smoking cessation, blood pressure and lipid control). Secondary prevention detects disease early (for example AAA screening for men in the year they turn 65). Tertiary prevention reduces harm in established disease (pulmonary rehabilitation, secondary prevention after myocardial infarction).

Conclusion. Most COPD, much coronary heart disease and most lung cancer are preventable in principle, because they are driven by modifiable exposures, especially smoking. Asthma, inherited conditions and the effects of ageing are much less preventable. Prevention also depends on social and structural factors (deprivation, housing, air quality, occupation), so it is not just a matter of individual choice.
questions.concept: Causes vs triggers and modifiable vs non-modifiable risk factors in common cardiorespiratory disease.

questions.q: On a standard 12-lead ECG recorded at 25 mm/s, the R–R interval in a regular rhythm is 4 large squares. What is the heart rate?
questions.why: At 25 mm/s a large square is 0.2 s, so 4 large squares is 0.8 s between beats. Rate = 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75/min, which is the same as 300 ÷ 4.
optWhy: 60/min would need 5 large squares (1.0 s).
100/min would need 3 large squares (0.6 s).
120/min would need 2.5 large squares (0.5 s).
300 is the numerator of the rule, not the answer.
questions.clue: 'R–R interval … 4 large squares' at 25 mm/s.
questions.concept: Calculating heart rate from a regular ECG.

followUp.q: A regular rhythm has 10 small squares between R waves at 25 mm/s. What is the rate?
followUp.why: 1,500 ÷ 10 = 150/min (10 small squares = 0.4 s; 60 ÷ 0.4 = 150). 30 comes from 300 ÷ 10, wrongly using the large-square rule with small squares.

questions.q: Spirometry in a 58-year-old shows FEV₁ 2.1 L (55% predicted), FVC 2.5 L (54% predicted), FEV₁/FVC 0.84. Which pattern does this most suggest?
options: A restrictive pattern, such as pulmonary fibrosis
An obstructive pattern, such as COPD
Large-airway obstruction from a tracheal tumour
questions.why: FEV₁/FVC = 2.1 ÷ 2.5 = 0.84, which is normal or high, while both volumes are reduced to about 55% of predicted. This proportional reduction is a restrictive pattern, as in interstitial lung disease, chest wall disease or neuromuscular weakness. Full lung volumes (low TLC) would confirm restriction.
optWhy: Correct: both volumes are reduced in proportion and the ratio is preserved (0.84), which suggests restriction.
Obstruction needs a ratio below 0.7; here it is 0.84.
Both FEV₁ and FVC are about 55% of predicted, which is not normal.
Asthma typically shows obstruction (low ratio) that improves with bronchodilator; no reversibility testing is given.
Fixed large-airway obstruction gives a flattened flow–volume loop and usually a reduced ratio, not proportionally reduced volumes.
questions.clue: FEV₁ and FVC both about 55% of predicted with a ratio of 0.84.
questions.concept: Distinguishing obstructive and restrictive spirometry.

followUp.q: A 66-year-old ex-smoker has post-bronchodilator FEV₁ 1.4 L (50% predicted) and FVC 3.0 L (85% predicted). Which pattern is this?
followUp.why: FEV₁/FVC = 1.4 ÷ 3.0 ≈ 0.47, well below 0.7: obstruction. FVC is near normal, so this is not restriction. A reduced FEV₁ is expected in obstruction and does not by itself mean a mixed defect.

questions.q: A 26-year-old is drowsy with deep, rapid breathing. ABG on air: pH 7.25, PaO₂ 12.8 kPa, PaCO₂ 3.0 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L; Na⁺ 136, Cl⁻ 100 mmol/L. What is the primary disturbance?
options: Raised anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
questions.why: pH 7.25 is acidaemic; bicarbonate is low (10 mmol/L), so the primary process is metabolic. PaCO₂ is low because deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing compensates. Check: pH ≈ 6.1 + log₁₀(10 ÷ (0.0307 × 22.5)) ≈ 6.1 + log₁₀(14.5) ≈ 7.26. Anion gap = 136 − (100 + 10) = 26 mmol/L, raised, suggesting added acid such as ketones (DKA) or lactate.
optWhy: Respiratory acidosis needs a raised PaCO₂; here it is low.
The pH is low (acidaemia), so the primary process cannot be an alkalosis.
The anion gap is 26 mmol/L, well above the typical 4–12 mmol/L.
Correct: low pH and low bicarbonate show a metabolic acidosis; low PaCO₂ is compensation; anion gap = 136 − (100 + 10) = 26 mmol/L, raised.
PaO₂ is normal (12.8 kPa on air), so there is no respiratory failure.
questions.clue: Low pH, low HCO₃⁻, low PaCO₂ and a calculable anion gap.
questions.concept: Stepwise ABG interpretation and the anion gap.

followUp.q: ABG on air: pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 8.0 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 28 mmol/L, PaO₂ 7.2 kPa. What is the primary disturbance?
options: Respiratory acidosis (type 2 respiratory failure) with some metabolic compensation
followUp.why: Low pH with raised PaCO₂ is a respiratory acidosis; PaO₂ below 8 kPa with PaCO₂ above 6 kPa is type 2 respiratory failure. A slightly raised bicarbonate suggests some renal compensation (a longer-standing component). Check: 6.1 + log₁₀(28 ÷ (0.0307 × 60)) ≈ 6.1 + log₁₀(15.2) ≈ 7.28.

questions.q: A 30-year-old with pleuritic pain has an ABG on air: PaO₂ 9.0 kPa, PaCO₂ 3.6 kPa. Taking alveolar PO₂ ≈ 20 − PaCO₂/0.8 kPa, what is the A–a gradient?
questions.why: PAO₂ ≈ 20 − 3.6/0.8 = 15.5 kPa; A–a gradient = 15.5 − 9.0 = 6.5 kPa, clearly raised for a young adult (normally under about 2 kPa, approximate). A raised gradient with hyperventilation and pleuritic pain should prompt consideration of pulmonary embolism.
optWhy: This subtracts PaO₂ from 20 without allowing for CO₂ (20 − 9.0).
A gradient of 2 kPa would need a PaO₂ of 13.5 kPa.
15.5 kPa is the alveolar PO₂, not the gradient.
4.5 kPa is PaCO₂ ÷ 0.8, one step of the calculation.
questions.clue: PaO₂ 9.0 kPa and PaCO₂ 3.6 kPa on air, with the alveolar gas equation given.
questions.concept: The A–a gradient separates gas-exchange failure from hypoventilation.

followUp.q: After an opioid overdose a 40-year-old has, on air, PaO₂ 7.5 kPa and PaCO₂ 9.0 kPa. What is the A–a gradient and what does it suggest?
options: About 1.25 kPa: normal, so hypoventilation explains the hypoxaemia
It cannot be calculated on air
followUp.why: PAO₂ = 20 − 9.0/0.8 = 20 − 11.25 = 8.75 kPa; gradient = 8.75 − 7.5 = 1.25 kPa, within normal. Hypoventilation lowers alveolar and arterial PO₂ together, so the gradient stays normal. 12.5 kPa forgets the CO₂ term (20 − 7.5).

questions.q: A 45-year-old has sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. The trachea is deviated to the left, the right chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds, BP 82/50 mmHg and heart rate 130/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds point to air in the right pleural space; tracheal deviation away from that side with hypotension and tachycardia show tension physiology, which impairs venous return. This is a clinical diagnosis needing immediate decompression rather than waiting for imaging.
optWhy: An effusion is stony dull, not hyper-resonant.
Collapse is dull and pulls the trachea towards the affected side.
Correct: a hyper-resonant, silent hemithorax with the trachea pushed away and shock indicates tension.
Consolidation is dull with bronchial breathing.
The signs are on the right; the trachea moves away from the tension side (to the left).
questions.clue: Hyper-resonant right chest, trachea to the left, BP 82/50.
questions.concept: Chest signs of air vs fluid vs solid lung, and tracheal position.

followUp.q: An older smoker has dullness, reduced breath sounds and reduced expansion over the left upper zone, with the trachea pulled to the left. Most likely cause?
options: Left upper lobe collapse, for example from an obstructing bronchial tumour
followUp.why: Dullness with volume loss pulling the trachea towards the affected side indicates collapse; in a smoker, an obstructing tumour is an important cause. Tension pneumothorax and massive effusion push the trachea away.

questions.q: Compare the typical chest examination findings in (i) right lower lobe consolidation, (ii) a large right pleural effusion and (iii) a right pneumothorax. For each, explain the physical basis of the percussion note and breath sounds.
markScheme: Consolidation: reduced expansion, dull percussion, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance/fremitus, possible crackles; trachea central
Basis: alveoli filled with exudate around patent airways; solid lung transmits large-airway sounds well and is dull
Effusion: reduced expansion, stony dull, reduced or absent breath sounds and vocal resonance; trachea central or pushed away if massive
Basis: fluid separates lung from chest wall and damps transmission of sound
Pneumothorax: reduced expansion, hyper-resonant, reduced or absent breath sounds and vocal resonance; trachea pushed away in tension
Basis: air in the pleural space resonates on percussion and insulates breath sounds
questions.modelAnswer: In right lower lobe consolidation, expansion is reduced on the right, percussion is dull, and there is bronchial breathing with increased vocal resonance and often coarse crackles; the trachea is central. The alveoli are filled with exudate but the airways stay open, so the solid lung conducts sound from the large airways to the chest wall, while the dense tissue sounds dull. With a large right pleural effusion, expansion is reduced, the percussion note is stony dull, and breath sounds and vocal resonance are reduced or absent; the trachea is central, or pushed to the left if the effusion is massive. The fluid lies between lung and chest wall, damping vibration and blocking transmission of sound. In a right pneumothorax, expansion is reduced, the percussion note is hyper-resonant, and breath sounds and vocal resonance are reduced or absent; in a tension pneumothorax the trachea is pushed away and the patient may be shocked. Air in the pleural space resonates when percussed and separates the lung from the chest wall, so breath sounds are poorly transmitted.
questions.concept: Chest signs reflect whether the pleural space or alveoli contain fluid, air or solid tissue.

questions.q: A 64-year-old man has 40 minutes of crushing central chest pain and sweating. Heart rate 46/min, BP 88/54 mmHg, SpO₂ 96% on air, chest clear, JVP raised. The 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF with ST depression in aVL; P waves at 80/min bear no fixed relation to regular QRS complexes at 44/min. (a) Interpret the ECG. (b) Explain the likely coronary anatomy and why he is bradycardic. (c) Explain why he is hypotensive with a raised JVP and clear lungs, and why this matters for treatment. (d) Outline the principles of immediate management according to UK guidance (no doses).
markScheme: (a) Inferior STEMI: ST elevation II, III, aVF with reciprocal ST depression in aVL
(a) Complete (third-degree) heart block: P waves and QRS complexes independent, ventricular rate slow
(b) Usually right coronary artery occlusion (circumflex in a minority); the RCA commonly supplies the AV node, so AV nodal ischaemia (and vagal reflexes) cause AV block
(c) Right ventricular infarction: poor RV output reduces LV filling → hypotension; RV failure raises JVP; lungs clear because the LV is not congested
(c) RV output is preload-dependent; nitrates (venodilators) and diuretics can cause profound hypotension
(d) ABCDE, oxygen only if hypoxaemic (BTS target 94–98%), antiplatelet therapy and analgesia per local protocol
(d) Immediate reperfusion: primary PCI if within 12 hours of onset and deliverable within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could be given (NICE NG185); otherwise fibrinolysis
(d) Treat the bradycardia if causing compromise (atropine/pacing per protocol); recognise that AV block in inferior MI is often transient
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The ECG shows ST elevation in the inferior leads (II, III and aVF) with reciprocal ST depression in aVL: an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. The atrial rate (80/min) and ventricular rate (44/min) are independent, with no fixed PR interval, so this is complete (third-degree) heart block with an escape rhythm.

(b) Inferior STEMI is usually caused by occlusion of the right coronary artery, and less often by the circumflex. In most people the RCA supplies the AV node, so ischaemia of the node (and vagal reflexes triggered by inferior ischaemia) can block conduction. AV block complicating inferior infarction is often transient once blood flow is restored.

(c) Hypotension with a raised JVP and clear lungs suggests right ventricular infarction, which commonly accompanies RCA occlusion. The damaged right ventricle cannot pump enough blood through the lungs, so left ventricular filling and cardiac output fall (hypotension), while blood backs up into the systemic veins (raised JVP). The lungs are clear because the left ventricle is not congested. The bradycardia from complete heart block further lowers cardiac output (CO = HR × SV). This matters because right ventricular output depends heavily on preload: venodilators such as nitrates, and diuretics, can cause profound hypotension. Right-sided chest leads (such as V4R) help confirm RV involvement.

(d) Management follows an ABCDE approach with senior and cardiology help. Oxygen is given only if he is hypoxaemic, aiming for the BTS target of 94–98% (his SpO₂ is 96% on air). Analgesia and antiplatelet therapy are given according to local ACS protocol. The priority is reperfusion: NICE NG185 recommends coronary angiography with primary PCI if he presents within 12 hours of symptom onset and PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given; otherwise fibrinolysis is offered. Bradycardia with shock is treated urgently according to the local adult bradycardia protocol (drug treatment and, if needed, pacing). Hypotension from RV infarction is managed by maintaining preload rather than with nitrates. Continuous monitoring is needed because arrhythmias are common. No doses are given here: follow local protocols and the BNF.
questions.concept: ECG territories, AV block and right ventricular infarction in inferior STEMI.

questions.q: What is the primary molecular target of statins?
questions.why: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase. With less cholesterol made inside hepatocytes, the cells upregulate LDL receptors and take up more LDL from the blood, lowering plasma LDL.
optWhy: COX-1 is the target of aspirin.
Correct: statins inhibit the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis.
Vitamin K epoxide reductase is the target of warfarin.
Statins increase LDL receptor numbers indirectly; they do not act on the receptor.
PCSK9 is targeted by other lipid-lowering drugs (monoclonal antibodies, inclisiran), not statins.
questions.clue: 'Primary molecular target of statins'.
questions.concept: Mechanism of statins.

followUp.q: Why does inhibiting cholesterol synthesis in liver cells lower blood LDL?
options: Hepatocytes upregulate LDL receptors and take up more LDL
followUp.why: Lower intracellular cholesterol activates the transcription programme that increases LDL receptor expression, so more LDL is cleared from plasma. The kidneys do not excrete cholesterol, and statins do not block intestinal absorption (ezetimibe does).

questions.q: A woman develops a persistent dry cough a few weeks after starting ramipril for hypertension. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Accumulation of bradykinin because ACE also breaks it down
Blockade of β2 receptors in the airways
Direct blockade of AT1 receptors in the lung
questions.why: ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II and also breaks down bradykinin. Ramipril therefore increases bradykinin, which sensitises airway cough reflexes. An ARB blocks the receptor without inhibiting ACE, so it is the usual alternative (NICE NG136).
optWhy: Correct: ACE (kininase II) degrades bradykinin; inhibiting it lets bradykinin accumulate.
β2 blockade is a feature of non-selective β-blockers, not ACE inhibitors.
ACE inhibitors tend to raise potassium, not lower it.
AT1 blockade is the action of ARBs, which rarely cause cough.
ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone and fluid retention.
questions.clue: Dry cough 'a few weeks after starting ramipril'.
questions.concept: ACE inhibitor cough is bradykinin-mediated.

followUp.q: A man taking an ACE inhibitor develops swelling of the lips and tongue. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to the tablet coating
followUp.why: Angioedema with ACE inhibitors is a rare but serious bradykinin-mediated effect, so the drug is stopped and not restarted. It is not typically IgE-mediated; hyperkalaemia does not cause facial swelling.

questions.q: A 70-year-old taking bisoprolol for angina is started on verapamil by mistake. Which adverse effect is the main concern?
options: Severe bradycardia, AV block and hypotension
questions.why: Verapamil is a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker that slows the SA and AV nodes and reduces contractility. Added to a β-blocker, the effects summate: severe bradycardia, AV block, hypotension and heart failure. The medicines information for intravenous verapamil lists simultaneous intravenous β-blockers as a contraindication and warns of additive effects with oral β-blockers.
optWhy: Ankle oedema is typical of dihydropyridines like amlodipine, and it is not the danger here.
Dry cough is an ACE inhibitor effect.
Hyperkalaemia is associated with ACE inhibitors, ARBs and MRAs.
Correct: both drugs slow SA and AV nodal conduction and reduce contractility.
Gout is associated with diuretics.
questions.clue: Bisoprolol plus 'verapamil'.
questions.concept: Additive negative chronotropy with β-blockers and rate-limiting CCBs.

followUp.q: A patient on bisoprolol needs a calcium-channel blocker for blood pressure. Which choice avoids the main interaction risk?
followUp.why: Amlodipine, a dihydropyridine, acts mainly on arterioles and has little effect on the AV node, so it is the usual choice with a β-blocker. Verapamil (and, to a lesser degree, diltiazem) add nodal slowing.

questions.q: A man with heart failure taking digoxin is started on a higher dose of furosemide. A week later he has nausea, confusion and frequent ventricular ectopics. Which change most directly explains his increased sensitivity to digoxin?
options: Hypokalaemia, so more digoxin binds to Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
questions.why: Furosemide blocks NKCC2 and increases distal sodium delivery, so more potassium is lost in the urine. Digoxin and potassium compete for the same site on Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, so hypokalaemia increases digoxin binding and its toxic effects (nausea, confusion, arrhythmias).
optWhy: Loop diuretics lower potassium, not raise it.
Sodium changes are not the main mechanism here.
Correct: loop diuretics lower K⁺, and low K⁺ increases digoxin binding and toxicity.
β1 receptor number is unrelated to digoxin toxicity.
Digoxin increases vagal tone; loss of it would not explain toxicity.
questions.clue: Digoxin plus increased furosemide, then nausea, confusion and ectopics.
questions.concept: Hypokalaemia potentiates digoxin.

followUp.q: Which other change would also make digoxin toxicity more likely?
options: A rise in serum potassium into the normal range
followUp.why: Digoxin is cleared mainly by the kidneys, so impaired kidney function raises its level. Correcting potassium reduces toxicity; stopping a loop diuretic would tend to raise potassium. Statins have no important interaction with digoxin in this sense.

questions.q: A 48-year-old man of Black African family origin without diabetes has confirmed stage 2 hypertension. According to NICE NG136, which step 1 drug class should be offered?
options: An ACE inhibitor combined with an ARB
questions.why: NICE NG136 offers a calcium-channel blocker first to adults aged 55 or over, and to adults of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin of any age, if they do not have type 2 diabetes. If an ACE-type drug is later added for this group, an ARB is considered in preference to an ACE inhibitor. Checked October 2026.
optWhy: Correct: people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin without type 2 diabetes start with a CCB at any age.
An ACE inhibitor is first for under-55s not of Black African or African-Caribbean origin, or for type 2 diabetes.
β-blockers are not a routine step 1 choice for hypertension in NICE guidance.
Loop diuretics are not used for uncomplicated hypertension.
NICE says not to combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB.
questions.clue: 'Black African family origin', 'without diabetes', age 48.
questions.concept: NICE NG136 step 1 choice by age, family origin and diabetes.

followUp.q: A 45-year-old white woman with type 2 diabetes has confirmed hypertension. Which step 1 drug class does NICE recommend?
followUp.why: For adults with type 2 diabetes, of any age or family origin, NICE NG136 offers an ACE inhibitor or ARB at step 1. A CCB is first for people aged 55 or over or of Black African or African-Caribbean origin without type 2 diabetes.

questions.q: β-blockers were once avoided in heart failure because they reduce contractility, yet selected β-blockers are now core treatment for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Explain this apparent paradox.
markScheme: In HFrEF, low cardiac output activates the sympathetic system and RAAS (neurohormonal model)
Chronic sympathetic activation is harmful: tachycardia, raised oxygen demand, arrhythmias, myocyte apoptosis and adverse remodelling; β1 receptor down-regulation
β-blockers block these effects: slower rate lengthens diastole (better filling and coronary perfusion), fewer arrhythmias, reverse remodelling and better EF over time
Acute negative inotropy is why they are started cautiously in stable patients and increased gradually
Evidence: selected agents improve survival and reduce admissions; NICE includes a β-blocker among the four HFrEF classes
questions.modelAnswer: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, the fall in cardiac output triggers compensatory activation of the sympathetic nervous system and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. In the short term this supports blood pressure, but if sustained it is harmful: tachycardia raises myocardial oxygen demand and shortens diastolic filling and coronary perfusion, catecholamines promote arrhythmias and myocyte death, and the ventricle remodels and dilates further. Selected β-blockers block these chronic effects. A slower heart rate improves filling and coronary flow, arrhythmias become less frequent, and over months the ventricle can reverse-remodel, with a rise in ejection fraction. Their acute negative inotropic effect is real, which is why they are started in stable patients and increased gradually. Trials of selected β-blockers showed lower mortality and fewer admissions, and NICE NG106 includes a β-blocker among the four medicine classes to offer in HFrEF.
questions.concept: Neurohormonal model: blocking chronic sympathetic activation improves outcomes in HFrEF.

questions.q: "In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, the drugs that make patients feel better are not always the drugs that make them live longer." Discuss, explaining the neurohormonal model of heart failure and how each major drug class acts. Do not give doses.
markScheme: Defines HFrEF (LVEF 40% or less) and explains the neurohormonal model: RAAS and sympathetic activation, initially compensatory, then harmful (vasoconstriction, salt and water retention, remodelling, fibrosis)
Loop diuretics: NKCC2 block, relieve congestion and symptoms quickly; no proven survival benefit; used at the lowest effective dose
ACE inhibitors/ARBs/ARNI: reduce angiotensin II and aldosterone effects; ARNI adds neprilysin inhibition (more natriuretic peptide); improve survival
β-blockers: block chronic sympathetic drive; improve survival despite initial negative inotropy
MRAs: block aldosterone (fibrosis, sodium retention); SGLT2 inhibitors: natriuresis and other effects; both improve outcomes
NICE NG106 (2025): offer all four classes, timing individualised; ARNI if symptoms persist
Digoxin: improves symptoms and reduces admissions but not mortality; adverse effects and interactions
Balanced conclusion with safety considerations (potassium, kidney function, hypotension) and the role of symptom relief
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement is broadly true, and the neurohormonal model explains why.

Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 40% or less in NICE NG106) begins with damage to the ventricle, often from coronary disease or hypertension. Falling cardiac output activates the sympathetic nervous system and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. In the short term this maintains blood pressure and filling. Sustained, it is harmful: angiotensin II and noradrenaline constrict arterioles and raise afterload, aldosterone retains salt and water and promotes fibrosis, catecholamines provoke arrhythmias and myocyte death, and the ventricle remodels and dilates. This creates a vicious circle in which the compensation drives the disease.

Drugs that mainly make patients feel better. Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, causing a natriuresis that quickly relieves pulmonary and peripheral congestion. Patients feel much less breathless, but these drugs do not interrupt the neurohormonal circle and have not been shown to improve survival; NICE advises using them at the lowest effective dose for congestion. Digoxin inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and increases vagal tone; it can improve symptoms and reduce admissions, but it has not been shown to reduce mortality, and its toxicity is worsened by hypokalaemia and kidney impairment.

Drugs that help patients live longer. ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II and aldosterone, lowering afterload and limiting remodelling; If an ACE inhibitor is not tolerated for reasons other than angioedema, NICE suggests switching to an ARNI; after ACE inhibitor angioedema, or if an ARNI is not tolerated, an ARB is considered. Sacubitril/valsartan (an ARNI) adds neprilysin inhibition, increasing natriuretic peptides, and NICE suggests considering it in place of the ACE inhibitor if symptoms persist; it must not be given with an ACE inhibitor. β-blockers block chronic sympathetic overactivity, slowing the heart, reducing arrhythmias and allowing reverse remodelling; they can make patients feel worse at first, which is why they are introduced gradually, yet they improve survival. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists block aldosterone’s effects on sodium retention and fibrosis. SGLT2 inhibitors increase sodium and glucose loss in the urine and improve outcomes in HFrEF independent of diabetes. NICE NG106 (updated September 2025) recommends offering all four classes (ACE inhibitor, β-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor), with timing and optimisation decided for the individual rather than in a fixed sequence.

Overlap and safety. The distinction is not absolute: prognostic drugs also improve symptoms over time, and relieving congestion matters for quality of life and keeps patients out of hospital. Combining RAAS blockers and MRAs risks hyperkalaemia and a fall in kidney function, so monitoring is essential; hypotension and bradycardia can limit β-blockers.

Conclusion. In HFrEF, symptom relief comes quickest from diuretics, while survival benefit comes from blocking the neurohormonal response and from SGLT2 inhibition. Good care uses both, guided by current NICE guidance and the BNF.
questions.concept: Symptomatic versus prognostic therapy in HFrEF and the neurohormonal model.

questions.q: The sensitivity of a diagnostic test is best defined as:
options: The proportion of people without the disease who test negative
The proportion of positive results that are true positives
The proportion of people with the disease who test positive
The proportion of negative results that are true negatives
The ratio of true positives to false positives
questions.why: Sensitivity is the proportion of people who have the disease who test positive: TP ÷ (TP + FN). It is a property of the test and does not depend on prevalence, unlike predictive values.
optWhy: This is specificity.
This is the positive predictive value.
Correct: sensitivity = TP ÷ (TP + FN).
This is the negative predictive value.
This ratio is not a standard measure of test accuracy.
questions.clue: 'Sensitivity … best defined as'.
questions.concept: Definitions of sensitivity, specificity and predictive values.

followUp.q: A test is used in a population where the disease becomes much more common. What happens to its sensitivity and PPV?
followUp.why: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test. Predictive values depend on prevalence: as prevalence rises, a positive result is more likely to be true, so PPV rises (and NPV falls).

questions.q: A 78-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has treated hypertension and had a transient ischaemic attack last year. He has no other conditions. What is his CHA₂DS₂-VASc score?
questions.why: CHA₂DS₂-VASc: congestive heart failure 1, hypertension 1, age 75 or over 2, diabetes 1, prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism 2, vascular disease 1, age 65–74 1, female sex 1. He scores 2 + 1 + 2 = 5. NICE NG196 recommends offering anticoagulation at 2 or more, taking bleeding risk into account.
optWhy: Correct: age 75 or over (2) + hypertension (1) + TIA (2) = 5.
This scores age as 1 and TIA as 1 (or misses one item).
This scores either age or TIA as 1 instead of 2.
This adds a point for female sex, which does not apply to him.
This counts only hypertension and age as 1 each, missing that age 75+ and TIA score 2.
questions.clue: Age 78, treated hypertension, TIA last year.
questions.concept: Scoring CHA₂DS₂-VASc.

followUp.q: A 68-year-old woman with AF has type 2 diabetes and no other risk factors. What is her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score?
followUp.why: Age 65–74 (1) + diabetes (1) + female sex (1) = 3. Under NICE NG196 anticoagulation would be offered (score 2 or more), considering bleeding risk.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman has pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness 10 days after knee surgery. Her two-level Wells score for PE is 6. Following NICE guidance, what is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
options: CT pulmonary angiography, with interim anticoagulation if it cannot be done immediately
D-dimer, and image only if positive
Chest X-ray and discharge if normal
Leg vein ultrasound for all patients first
Repeat the Wells score in 24 hours
questions.why: NICE NG158 classes a two-level PE Wells score over 4 as "PE likely" and recommends CTPA immediately if possible, or interim anticoagulation if imaging is delayed. If CTPA is unsuitable (for example contrast allergy or severe kidney impairment), a V/Q scan is considered.
optWhy: Correct: a score over 4 means PE is likely, so NICE NG158 recommends CTPA.
D-dimer first is for a score of 4 or less.
A normal chest X-ray does not exclude PE.
Leg ultrasound is considered if imaging is negative and DVT is suspected, not as the routine first test.
Delaying assessment risks harm; interim anticoagulation is offered if imaging is delayed.
questions.clue: Wells score '6' after recent surgery.
questions.concept: Two-level Wells score directs CTPA vs D-dimer.

followUp.q: A 32-year-old has mild pleuritic pain with a two-level Wells score of 1.5. What does NICE recommend first?
followUp.why: A score of 4 or less means PE is unlikely: offer a D-dimer test. A negative result makes PE unlikely; a positive one leads to imaging.

questions.q: A D-dimer test with sensitivity 95% and specificity 50% is used in 1,000 people in whom the prevalence of PE is 10%. What is the positive predictive value?
questions.why: Of 1,000 people, 100 have PE: 95 test positive (TP), 5 negative (FN). Of 900 without PE, 50% test negative (TN 450) and 450 test positive (FP). PPV = 95 ÷ (95 + 450) ≈ 17%; NPV = 450 ÷ 455 ≈ 99%. This is why D-dimer is used to rule out, not rule in.
optWhy: 95% is the sensitivity, not the PPV.
Correct: TP 95, FP 450, so PPV = 95 ÷ 545 ≈ 17%.
50% is the specificity.
About 99% is the NPV (450 ÷ 455).
10% is the prevalence (pre-test probability).
questions.clue: Sensitivity 95%, specificity 50%, prevalence 10% in 1,000 people.
questions.concept: Constructing a 2 × 2 table and calculating predictive values.

followUp.q: The same test is used where the prevalence of PE is 40%. What is the PPV now?
followUp.why: 400 have PE: TP 380, FN 20. 600 do not: TN 300, FP 300. PPV = 380 ÷ 680 ≈ 56%; NPV = 300 ÷ 320 ≈ 94%. Higher prevalence raises PPV and lowers NPV; sensitivity is unchanged at 95%.

questions.q: A ward patient has respiratory rate 25/min, SpO₂ 95% on air, systolic BP 105 mmHg, pulse 115/min, is alert, and has a temperature of 38.4 °C. Using NEWS2 (SpO₂ Scale 1), what is the aggregate score and the indicated response?
options: 3: low–medium risk, urgent ward-based review only
questions.why: NEWS2 Scale 1: respiration 25 or more scores 3; SpO₂ 94–95% scores 1; air 0; systolic 101–110 scores 1; pulse 111–130 scores 2; alert 0; temperature 38.1–39.0 °C scores 1. Total 8. RCP guidance treats an aggregate of 7 or more as high clinical risk needing an emergency response from a team with critical-care competencies.
optWhy: Correct: RR 25 (3) + SpO₂ 95% (1) + air (0) + systolic 105 (1) + pulse 115 (2) + alert (0) + temperature 38.4 °C (1) = 8.
This leaves out the 3 points for a respiratory rate of 25 or more.
This counts only the single red score for respiratory rate and ignores the other parameters.
This overcounts, for example scoring the pulse as 3 (that needs 131 or more) and the temperature as 2 (39.1 °C or more).
This scores the respiratory rate as 2, the band for 21–24.
questions.clue: Six observations given, on air.
questions.concept: Calculating NEWS2 and the linked clinical response.

followUp.q: A patient scores 0 on every NEWS2 parameter except new confusion. What is the score and response?
options: 0: no action, because confusion is not scored
3: a single red score, prompting urgent ward-based review
followUp.why: New confusion scores 3 in the ACVPU scale. A single parameter scoring 3 is a red score that RCP guidance links to an urgent ward-based response, even when the total is low. Chronic, unchanged confusion is not scored.

questions.q: In a 5-year trial, a new lipid-lowering drug reduced the rate of major cardiovascular events from 10% in the placebo group to 7.5% in the treatment group. Calculate the absolute risk reduction, relative risk reduction and number needed to treat, and explain why the same relative risk reduction can mean very different benefit for different patients.
markScheme: NNT = 1 ÷ 0.025 = 40 over 5 years
Absolute benefit depends on baseline risk: at a 2% baseline the same 25% RRR gives ARR 0.5% and NNT 200
So treatment decisions (e.g. NICE’s QRISK3 thresholds) and shared decisions should use absolute risk; RRR alone can mislead
questions.modelAnswer: The absolute risk reduction is the difference in event rates: 10% − 7.5% = 2.5%. The relative risk reduction is the ARR divided by the control rate: 2.5 ÷ 10 = 25%. The number needed to treat is 1 ÷ ARR = 1 ÷ 0.025 = 40, so 40 people need treating for 5 years to prevent one major event. A relative risk reduction is often roughly constant across risk groups, but absolute benefit depends on baseline risk. For a low-risk person with a 2% 5-year event rate, a 25% RRR lowers it to 1.5%: ARR 0.5% and NNT 200. A high-risk person gains far more from the same drug. This is why risk is estimated (for example with QRISK3) before offering preventive treatment, and why patients should be given absolute figures when making shared decisions.
questions.concept: ARR, RRR and NNT, and why absolute risk matters.

questions.q: Doris, 74, is brought in with 3 days of productive cough and fever. Today she is newly muddled about the date and place. Respiratory rate 26/min, SpO₂ 91% on air, BP 102/58 mmHg, pulse 108/min, temperature 38.6 °C. Urea 9.1 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. (a) Calculate her CURB65 score and state what NICE NG250 indicates about severity and place of care. (b) Calculate her NEWS2 and state the expected response. (c) Explain how an ABCDE approach would structure her initial management (principles only, no doses). (d) Identify two cognitive biases that could lead to error in her care and how to guard against them.
markScheme: (a) CURB65: confusion 1, urea over 7 mmol/L 1, RR under 30 so 0, BP: diastolic 58 (60 or less) 1, age 65 or over 1 = 4
(a) 3–5 = high severity (NICE NG250): inpatient care, consider critical care referral; chest X-ray and antibiotics within 4 hours of presentation
(b) NEWS2 (Scale 1): RR 26 = 3, SpO₂ 91 = 3, air 0, SBP 102 = 1, pulse 108 = 1, new confusion = 3, temperature 38.6 = 1; total 12: high, emergency response

(c) ABCDE: airway; breathing (oxygen to BTS target 94–98% unless at risk of hypercapnia, sputum and blood cultures); circulation (IV access, bloods including lactate, fluids for hypotension, sepsis pathway); disability (glucose, confusion); exposure; reassess and escalate early
(c) Antibiotics promptly per local guidance; SBAR handover to senior; shared decisions considering her wishes
(d) Anchoring/premature closure (e.g. labelling confusion as dementia or "just an infection" and missing sepsis or another cause); availability bias
(d) Safeguards: ask "what else?", use structured scores, review trends, senior review, check baseline cognition with family
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) CURB65. Confusion (new disorientation): 1. Urea 9.1 mmol/L (over 7): 1. Respiratory rate 26/min (not 30 or more): 0. Blood pressure: systolic 102 is not under 90, but diastolic 58 is 60 or less: 1. Age 74 (65 or over): 1. Total 4. NICE NG250 classes 3–5 as high severity (mortality risk over 15%), and since 2025 recommends inpatient care with referral to critical care if appropriate for scores of 3 or more. NICE also expects systems that allow a chest X-ray and the start of antibiotics within 4 hours of presentation to hospital.

(b) NEWS2 (Scale 1, on air). Respiratory rate 26 (25 or more): 3. SpO₂ 91% (91 or less): 3. Air: 0. Systolic BP 102 (101–110): 1. Pulse 108 (101–110): 1. New confusion: 3. Temperature 38.6 °C (38.1–39.0): 1. Total 12. An aggregate of 7 or more is high clinical risk, needing an emergency response from a team with critical-care skills. Several individual parameters also score 3.

(c) ABCDE. The Resuscitation Council UK approach assesses and treats in order, dealing with life-threatening problems as they are found and reassessing after each step. Airway: is she talking? Breathing: rate, effort, chest signs and saturation; give oxygen to the BTS target of 94–98% (88–92% only if she is at risk of hypercapnic failure, which should be checked); obtain an ABG if indicated. Circulation: pulse, BP, capillary refill, urine output; IV access, blood cultures, full blood count, kidney function, CRP and lactate; treat hypotension with fluids following a sepsis pathway. Disability: conscious level, glucose and her confusion (delirium is likely). Exposure: temperature, other sources of infection, skin. Start antibiotics promptly according to local guidance. Call for senior help early, hand over using SBAR, and involve Doris and her family in decisions about the level of care, respecting any advance care plan. Reassess frequently and repeat NEWS2.

(d) Cognitive biases. Anchoring and premature closure: her confusion might be attributed to presumed dementia, or the label "chest infection" might stop the team looking for sepsis or another cause (for example hypoxia, hypoglycaemia or a stroke). Availability bias: a recent run of mild chest infections might lead staff to underestimate her severity. Guards include asking "what else could this be?", checking baseline cognition with her family, using structured scores (CURB65, NEWS2) and their trends rather than impressions, early senior review and explicit handover of uncertainties.
questions.concept: Applying CURB65, NEWS2 and ABCDE in pneumonia, and recognising bias.

cases.title: Breathless and swollen ankles

steps.text: A 71-year-old retired engineer with long-standing hypertension and a myocardial infarction 4 years ago has 6 months of worsening breathlessness. He now sleeps on three pillows and twice a week wakes at night gasping. His ankles swell by evening.

ask.q: Which mechanism best explains needing three pillows and waking breathless at night?
options: Bronchoconstriction from a nocturnal rise in adrenaline
Lying flat increases venous return to a failing left ventricle, raising pulmonary venous pressure and causing interstitial oedema
ask.why: Orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea reflect redistribution of blood from the legs to the chest when lying down. A failing left ventricle cannot handle the extra preload, so left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rise and fluid leaks into the lung interstitium (Starling forces). Adrenaline falls rather than rises at night; tracheal compression is not the mechanism; COPD-related hypoventilation would not explain the relief from sitting up and the ankle swelling.

steps.text: Pulse 96/min irregularly irregular, BP 148/88 mmHg, JVP raised 6 cm, bibasal fine crackles, pitting oedema to mid-shin. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 100/min and Q waves in V1–V4.

ask.q: Which test is the most useful next step to support a diagnosis of heart failure before echocardiography?
ask.why: A natriuretic peptide is released from stretched ventricular myocardium; a normal level makes heart failure unlikely, and a raised level supports referral for echocardiography and specialist assessment. D-dimer is for suspected VTE; troponin for suspected acute myocardial injury; amylase is irrelevant.

steps.text: NT-proBNP is markedly raised. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30% and an anterior wall motion abnormality.

ask.q: How is this heart failure classified, and which medicine classes does NICE recommend offering for prognosis?
options: HFpEF: a loop diuretic alone, because it improves survival
HFrEF (LVEF 40% or less): an ACE inhibitor, a β-blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor
HFrEF: a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker to slow the AF
ask.why: An LVEF of 30% is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. NICE NG106 (updated 2025) recommends offering an ACE inhibitor, a β-blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor, with timing individualised. Loop diuretics relieve congestion but do not improve survival. Rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers such as verapamil reduce contractility and are generally avoided in HFrEF.

steps.text: He is also in atrial fibrillation. He has hypertension, heart failure, vascular disease (previous MI) and is 71.

ask.q: What is his CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, and what does NICE NG196 recommend?
options: 3: no anticoagulation because of his age
5: anticoagulation only if ORBIT is low
4: offer anticoagulation, taking bleeding risk into account
ask.why: Heart failure 1 + hypertension 1 + vascular disease 1 + age 65–74 1 = 4. NICE offers anticoagulation at 2 or more, considering bleeding risk with ORBIT, which is used to address modifiable risks rather than, by itself, to withhold treatment. Aspirin alone is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF.

steps.text: Outcome: he is started on guideline-directed treatment with careful monitoring of potassium, kidney function, blood pressure and heart rate, a diuretic for congestion, anticoagulation after discussing benefits and risks, and referral for cardiac rehabilitation and education. No doses are given here.

debrief: Orthopnoea and PND come from increased venous return to a failing left ventricle raising pulmonary venous pressure.
A normal natriuretic peptide makes heart failure unlikely; echocardiography classifies it by ejection fraction.
In HFrEF, NICE recommends offering an ACE inhibitor, β-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor; diuretics treat congestion, not prognosis.
AF with heart failure carries high stroke risk; CHA₂DS₂-VASc guides anticoagulation and ORBIT guides correction of bleeding risks.

cases.title: Breathless after knee surgery

steps.text: A 30-year-old woman, known to have anxiety, attends the emergency department with 1 day of breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She had knee surgery 2 weeks ago and has been mostly on the sofa since.

ask.q: A colleague says, "It’s another panic attack." Which thinking error is this, and what should you do?
options: Anchoring and premature closure: ask what else this could be and list must-not-miss diagnoses such as PE
Availability bias: order every test available
No error: anxiety is the most likely diagnosis in her
ask.why: Fixing on a previous label (anchoring) and stopping the search (premature closure) risks missing PE, which is dangerous and plausible after surgery and immobility (Virchow’s triad). Anxiety can only be diagnosed after dangerous causes have been considered.

steps.text: Observations: RR 24/min, SpO₂ 94% on air, pulse 112/min, BP 124/76 mmHg, temperature 37.4 °C. Chest clear; no leg swelling. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray normal.

ask.q: Her two-level PE Wells score is 6 (heart rate over 100, surgery in the past 4 weeks, PE judged the most likely diagnosis). What is the next step under NICE NG158?
options: CTPA immediately, with interim anticoagulation if imaging is delayed
D-dimer first, image only if positive
Discharge because the chest X-ray is normal
ask.why: A score over 4 means PE is likely, so NICE recommends CTPA; if it cannot be done straight away, interim anticoagulation is offered. D-dimer first is for scores of 4 or less. A normal chest X-ray does not exclude PE; V/Q scanning is used if CTPA is unsuitable.

steps.text: An ABG on air: pH 7.50, PaO₂ 9.0 kPa, PaCO₂ 3.6 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 21 mmol/L.

ask.q: Taking alveolar PO₂ ≈ 20 − PaCO₂/0.8 kPa, what does the A–a gradient show?
options: About 6.5 kPa: raised, indicating a gas-exchange problem such as V/Q mismatch
About 1 kPa: normal, so anxiety-related hyperventilation explains everything
About 11 kPa: this ignores the CO₂ term
It cannot be calculated without an FiO₂ of 100%
ask.why: PAO₂ = 20 − 3.6/0.8 = 15.5 kPa; A–a gradient = 15.5 − 9.0 = 6.5 kPa, clearly raised. Hyperventilation from anxiety alone would give a normal gradient. The respiratory alkalosis (high pH, low PaCO₂, normal bicarbonate) reflects hyperventilation. Check: 6.1 + log₁₀(21 ÷ (0.0307 × 27)) ≈ 6.1 + log₁₀(25.3) ≈ 7.50.

steps.text: Outcome: CTPA shows bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli. She is haemodynamically stable and anticoagulation is started per local guidance after discussing the options with her. No doses are given here.

debrief: Ask "what else could this be?" before accepting a benign label, especially when a must-not-miss diagnosis fits.
NICE uses the two-level PE Wells score: over 4 → CTPA; 4 or fewer → D-dimer first.
A raised A–a gradient shows a gas-exchange problem; pure hyperventilation keeps it normal.
Recent surgery and immobility act through stasis and hypercoagulability in Virchow’s triad.

osce.title: Cardiovascular examination
steps: Clean your hands, introduce yourself, confirm the patient’s name and date of birth, explain the examination, gain consent and ask about pain
Position the patient at about 45° with the chest exposed appropriately; offer a chaperone
General inspection from the end of the bed: breathlessness, colour, scars, and clues nearby (oxygen, GTN spray, medicines)
Hands: temperature, capillary refill, clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, tendon xanthomata
Radial pulse rate and rhythm; compare both radial pulses; check for a collapsing pulse after asking about shoulder pain
Blood pressure (measure it, or state that you would)
Face: conjunctival pallor, xanthelasma, corneal arcus, central cyanosis, dentition
Neck: jugular venous pressure at 45°, then carotid pulse character, one side at a time
Chest inspection: scars (e.g. sternotomy), pacemaker, visible pulsation, deformity
Palpation: apex beat (normally about the fifth intercostal space, mid-clavicular line), heaves and thrills

Auscultation: mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary and aortic areas, timing with the carotid pulse; add manoeuvres (left lateral for mitral stenosis, sitting forward in held expiration for aortic regurgitation); listen over the carotids
Lung bases for crackles, then sacrum and ankles for pitting oedema
Thank the patient, clean your hands, summarise findings and suggest next steps (e.g. full observations, 12-lead ECG, echocardiogram)
tips: Time murmurs against the carotid pulse to separate systole from diastole.
Feel each carotid gently and separately.
Relate findings to physiology: a raised JVP with ankle oedema suggests right-sided congestion.
Follow your own medical school’s mark scheme where its order differs.

osce.title: Respiratory examination
steps: Clean your hands, introduce yourself, confirm identity, explain the examination, gain consent and ask about pain
Position the patient at about 45° with the chest exposed appropriately; offer a chaperone
General inspection: breathlessness at rest, accessory muscle use, pursed-lip breathing, cough, and clues nearby (inhalers, oxygen, sputum pot)
Hands: clubbing, peripheral cyanosis, tar staining, wasting, and a flapping tremor (CO₂ retention)
Pulse and respiratory rate (count breaths discreetly for a full minute)
Face and neck: central cyanosis, conjunctival pallor, jugular venous pressure
Trachea position (warn the patient first) and cricosternal distance
Chest inspection: shape, symmetry, scars
Palpation: expansion on both sides and the apex beat
Percussion: compare both sides in each zone, including the axillae; tactile vocal fremitus
Auscultation: compare both sides for breath sounds and added sounds, then vocal resonance
Lymph nodes of the neck and supraclavicular fossae
Repeat expansion, percussion and auscultation on the back
Ankles for oedema and calves for signs of DVT
Thank the patient, clean your hands, summarise and suggest next steps (e.g. SpO₂, peak flow, spirometry, chest X-ray, ABG if indicated)
tips: Always compare like with like on both sides.
Dull = fluid or solid lung; hyper-resonant = air.
Tracheal deviation helps separate push (tension, massive effusion) from pull (collapse, fibrosis).
Follow your own medical school’s mark scheme where its order differs.

interpret.title: Breathless at high altitude
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A healthy 20-year-old has trekked rapidly to 4,500 m and is breathless on minimal exertion. An arterial sample is taken on air at altitude. Which interpretation fits best? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK sea-level ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: Respiratory alkalosis from hypoxic stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors, with early renal compensation
Normal gas exchange: these values are expected at sea level
interpret.why: Low inspired PO₂ at altitude lowers PaO₂ (6.9 kPa) enough to stimulate the peripheral chemoreceptors strongly, so she hyperventilates. PaCO₂ falls (3.8 kPa ≈ 28.5 mmHg) and pH rises (7.48): a respiratory alkalosis. Check: pH ≈ 6.1 + log₁₀(21 ÷ (0.0307 × 28.5)) ≈ 6.1 + log₁₀(24.0) ≈ 7.48. Bicarbonate slightly below range (21 mmol/L) shows the kidneys beginning to excrete bicarbonate, which over days brings pH back towards normal.
optWhy: In a metabolic alkalosis bicarbonate would be raised; here it is slightly low and PaCO₂ is low.
Correct: low PaO₂ drives hyperventilation via the carotid bodies, lowering PaCO₂ and raising pH; bicarbonate is slightly low as the kidneys start to compensate.
Type 2 failure needs a raised PaCO₂; here PaCO₂ is low because she is hyperventilating.
In a metabolic acidosis pH would be low; here it is high.
A PaO₂ of 6.9 kPa is far below sea-level values; the low inspired oxygen at altitude explains it.

interpret.title: Lipids in a young man with a family history
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 34-year-old man’s father died of a myocardial infarction at 46. He has thickened Achilles tendons. He does not smoke and has no diabetes. Fasting lipids are shown. What is the most appropriate interpretation? (Reference ranges are typical adult UK values and vary by laboratory.)
options: Low cardiovascular risk because HDL is normal: no action needed
Calculate QRISK3 and offer a statin only if the score is 10% or more
Secondary hyperlipidaemia from hypothyroidism is certain
Probable familial hypercholesterolaemia: refer for specialist assessment and offer testing to first-degree relatives
interpret.why: Non-HDL = 9.2 − 1.3 = 7.9 mmol/L, and LDL is 7.0 mmol/L (Friedewald check: 9.2 − 1.3 − 1.9/2.2 ≈ 7.0). Total cholesterol above about 7.5 mmol/L with tendon xanthomata and a parent with early coronary disease makes FH likely. It is usually autosomal dominant, so each first-degree relative has a 50% chance of carrying it. A risk tool is not used for FH (NICE NG238).
optWhy: A normal HDL does not offset an LDL of 7.0 mmol/L; his risk is high.
NICE says not to use a risk tool in FH, because it underestimates risk.
Secondary causes should be excluded (e.g. thyroid function), but nothing here makes hypothyroidism certain; xanthomata and family history point to FH.
Correct: very high total and LDL cholesterol with tendon xanthomata and premature coronary death in a parent strongly suggest FH.
Triglycerides are within the typical range; LDL is the main abnormality.

interpret.title: Rate and intervals on a lead II strip
interpret.q: Recorded at 25 mm/s: a regular rhythm with a P wave before every QRS. The R–R interval is 15 small squares, the PR interval 4 small squares and the QRS 2 small squares. Which description fits?
options: Sinus rhythm at 100 beats/min with normal intervals
interpret.why: R–R = 15 × 0.04 = 0.6 s, so rate = 60 ÷ 0.6 = 100/min (1,500 ÷ 15). PR = 0.16 s and QRS = 0.08 s are normal, with a P before every QRS: sinus rhythm at the upper limit of normal.
optWhy: Correct: R–R 15 × 0.04 = 0.6 s → 100/min; PR 0.16 s and QRS 0.08 s are normal.
150/min would need an R–R of 10 small squares (0.4 s).
PR 4 small squares = 0.16 s, under the 0.20 s limit.
20/min comes from 300 ÷ 15, wrongly using the large-square rule with small squares.
AF has no P waves and an irregular rhythm; this rhythm is regular with P waves.

interpret.title: Irregular palpitations
interpret.q: A 72-year-old has palpitations. The rhythm strip shows no distinct P waves and irregularly irregular narrow QRS complexes, 20 of them in 10 seconds. Which interpretation fits?
options: Atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 200/min
Atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 120/min
interpret.why: Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm is atrial fibrillation. For an irregular rhythm, count complexes on a 10-second strip and multiply by 6: 20 × 6 = 120/min. The next steps include assessing stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) and bleeding risk.
optWhy: 200/min multiplies the 10-second count by 10 instead of 6.
Flutter shows sawtooth flutter waves and, with 2:1 block, a regular ventricular rate around 150/min.
Correct: no P waves, irregularly irregular, 20 × 6 = 120/min.
Sinus arrhythmia has P waves before each QRS and varies with breathing.
VT is a regular broad-complex tachycardia; these complexes are narrow and irregular.

interpret.title: Chest pain with a slow pulse
interpret.q: A 64-year-old has crushing chest pain. This lead II strip shows regular P waves at 80/min and regular narrow QRS complexes at 40/min with no fixed PR interval, and the ST segment is raised. The 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF with ST depression in aVL. Which interpretation fits best?
options: Anterior STEMI with first-degree heart block
Inferior STEMI with Mobitz type II block
Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response
Inferior STEMI with complete heart block
interpret.why: ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal change in aVL is an inferior STEMI, usually from right coronary artery occlusion. P waves (80/min) and QRS complexes (40/min) are independent: complete heart block, because the RCA often supplies the AV node. Because the block is at the level of the AV node, the escape rhythm here is junctional, so the QRS stays narrow.
optWhy: Anterior STEMI involves V1–V4; first-degree block has a constant PR with every P conducted.
Mobitz II has a constant PR with intermittently dropped beats, not complete dissociation.
In sinus bradycardia every P is conducted with a fixed PR, and the 12-lead changes are territorial with reciprocal depression.
AF has no organised P waves; here regular P waves are visible.
Correct: inferior lead ST elevation with independent P waves and slow QRS complexes.

interpret.title: Breathless ex-smoker
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 63-year-old ex-smoker (40 pack-years) has exertional breathlessness and a morning cough. Post-bronchodilator spirometry is shown. Which interpretation fits best? (Predicted values are illustrative.)
options: Restrictive defect consistent with pulmonary fibrosis
Persistent airflow obstruction consistent with COPD
Mixed obstructive and restrictive defect proven by these results
interpret.why: FEV₁/FVC = 1.5 ÷ 2.9 = 0.52, below 0.7 after bronchodilator: persistent obstruction. With a 40 pack-year history and symptoms, this is consistent with COPD (NICE NG115). FEV₁ at 55% of predicted indicates moderate airflow limitation. NICE also recommends a chest X-ray, full blood count and BMI at diagnosis.
optWhy: Restriction would have a normal or high ratio; here it is low.
Correct: post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC = 1.5 ÷ 2.9 ≈ 0.52, below 0.7, with a typical history.
FEV₁ is 55% of predicted and the ratio is low.
The result is post-bronchodilator and still obstructed; asthma is suggested by variable, reversible obstruction.
A modestly reduced FVC is expected with air trapping; proving restriction needs lung volumes (TLC).

interpret.title: Bloods after a change in heart failure medicines
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 76-year-old with HFrEF takes digoxin. His loop diuretic was increased 10 days ago. He now has nausea, confusion and frequent ectopics. Which result best explains his symptoms? (Reference ranges are typical adult UK values and vary by laboratory.)
options: Raised urea from dehydration alone, with no effect on digoxin
Low potassium increasing digoxin binding to Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
Normal potassium, so digoxin toxicity is excluded
interpret.why: Potassium 2.9 mmol/L is low after the diuretic increase; low K⁺ lets more digoxin bind to Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, increasing its toxic effects. Raised creatinine (148 µmol/L) and urea suggest reduced kidney function, which also raises digoxin levels. These findings fit digoxin toxicity; a digoxin level and ECG would follow.
optWhy: Sodium 134 mmol/L is slightly low, not high.
Urea and creatinine are raised, which is relevant: reduced kidney function also raises digoxin levels.
Correct: potassium 2.9 mmol/L is low, and hypokalaemia potentiates digoxin.
Creatinine is raised, not low; impaired excretion raises the digoxin level.
Potassium is low (2.9 mmol/L), not normal.

interpret.title: Observations on a medical ward
interpret.rangeNote: Normal ranges shown are typical adult values; NEWS2 scoring bands are set by the RCP chart.
interpret.q: A 68-year-old admitted with cellulitis has these observations. Using NEWS2 Scale 1, what is the aggregate score and the indicated response? (Normal ranges are typical adult values.)
options: 5: medium risk, urgent response by a clinician skilled in assessing acutely ill patients
2: low risk, no change in monitoring
5: low risk, because no single parameter scores 3
interpret.why: NEWS2 Scale 1: respiration 21–24 scores 2; SpO₂ 94–95% scores 1; on air 0; systolic BP 101–110 scores 1; pulse 91–110 scores 1; alert 0; temperature 37.1–38.0 °C scores 0. Total 5: medium clinical risk, the RCP key threshold for an urgent response, with review by a clinician competent in acute illness and increased monitoring.
optWhy: Correct: RR 22 (2) + SpO₂ 95% (1) + air (0) + SBP 108 (1) + pulse 98 (1) + alert (0) + temperature 37.8 °C (0) = 5.
This misses the points for SpO₂ and systolic BP.
This overcounts; no parameter here scores 3.
This counts only the pulse and BP.
An aggregate of 5 is medium risk and the key threshold for an urgent response, whether or not a single parameter scores 3.
